questions.question: A larger context window means Claude uses all of its content equally well, so adding more material never hurts.
questions.explanation: Anthropic describes context rot: accuracy and recall degrade as more tokens accumulate, so more context is not automatically better.

questions.question: Each Project has its own memory, and inside a Project Claude does not use memory from other Projects.
questions.explanation: Project memory is kept separately; inside a Project Claude uses that Project's memory plus account memory from non-Project chats, never another Project's.

questions.question: Memory for a particular chat can still be switched off after the conversation is already underway.
questions.explanation: The per-chat memory setting must be chosen before the first message and cannot be changed once the chat starts.

questions.question: An operations manager has pasted rough notes from interviews with three department heads and wants a requirements list for a new intake process. What is the best use of Claude here?
options: Ask Claude to write the final requirements document and circulate it to the three departments as approved
Ask Claude to list each requirement with its source, flagging conflicts and assumptions for the interviewees to confirm
Ask Claude to keep only the requirements that all three department heads mentioned and discard the rest
Ask Claude to treat the most senior department head's notes as the baseline and ignore the differences
questions.explanation: Claude is good at organizing messy input and surfacing conflicts, but requirements must be confirmed by the people who own the need, and naming sources and assumptions makes that review quick. Circulating an unreviewed document, keeping only the overlap, or deferring to seniority each hides real needs or disagreements.

questions.question: A project manager's draft requirements include the line 'The new portal must be fast and easy to use.' What should she ask Claude to do with it?
options: Rewrite the line in stronger wording so that it reads as more convincing to the sponsors
Delete the line, because a requirement that has no numbers in it cannot be tested
Replace the line with typical industry figures that Claude chooses and treats as agreed
Propose measurable versions, such as a target page-load time and a task-completion rate, for the stakeholders to confirm
questions.explanation: Words like 'fast' and 'easy' mean different things to different readers, so an ambiguity check turns them into measurable proposals that stakeholders then accept or adjust. Stronger wording adds no precision, deleting the line loses a real need, and figures that Claude picks and declares agreed skip the people who must agree.

questions.question: A team is choosing its first use case for Claude. Which candidate is the best fit?
options: Sorting and summarizing 300 weekly customer emails into themes for the team's own trend review
Deciding which of 40 applicants to reject and sending the rejection emails automatically
Calculating payroll deductions for all employees and paying out the figures straight from Claude's answer
Analyzing a folder of restricted client contracts through a personal account to save time
questions.explanation: A good first use case is frequent, text-heavy, easy to check and low in consequence, and the email-themes task has all four. Automatic rejections are high-risk decisions about people, payroll figures must be exact and verified, and restricted contracts must not be handled through a personal account.

questions.question: A team has a list of 12 ideas for using Claude and wants to decide where to start. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?
options: Ask Claude to pick the single best idea and treat its choice as the decision
Start with whichever idea is the most exciting and score the others later if time allows
Give Claude the scoring criteria, such as time saved, effort, data risk and ease of checking, and review its scores together
Ask Claude to build prototypes of all twelve at once so that nothing is lost by choosing
questions.explanation: Claude can score and sort a long list quickly once it has explicit criteria, but the criteria and the decision itself belong to the team, who know the real constraints. Letting Claude decide, following excitement, or building everything skips prioritization.

questions.question: A project manager asks Claude, 'Make me a launch plan,' and gets a generic checklist. Which follow-up request is most likely to produce something she can use?
options: Ask for a longer checklist of at least 50 items so that nothing is missed
Ask Claude to use a more confident tone so that the plan can be shared with the team straight away
Supply the goal, launch date, team size, known dependencies and constraints, and ask for a work breakdown with risks
Ask Claude to repeat the same plan as a table, since structure is what makes a plan specific
questions.explanation: A plan is only as specific as the facts it is built from. Giving Claude the goal, date, capacity, dependencies and constraints lets it produce a tailored breakdown and surface risks, which the manager then checks with the team. More items, a different tone or a table change the packaging, not the content.

questions.question: A finance team describes its invoice-approval process and asks Claude for improvements. Which plan makes the best use of Claude's suggestions?
options: Have Claude map the steps and flag delays and rework, then pilot the most promising change and compare it with current timings
Adopt all of Claude's suggestions together, because Claude has considered the whole process
Ask Claude to redesign the process from scratch without referring to today's steps, then switch over at month end
Choose the suggestions that Claude states most confidently, since confidence reflects how well the evidence supports them
questions.explanation: Claude sees only the process as described, so its suggestions are hypotheses. Piloting the most promising change and measuring it against current timings turns a suggestion into evidence. Adopting everything at once makes results impossible to attribute, a from-scratch redesign ignores constraints Claude may not know, and confidence is not evidence.

questions.question: From a written description of a hiring process, Claude names interview scheduling as the likely bottleneck. What should the team do before redesigning anything?
options: Redesign the scheduling step straight away, since Claude has identified it
Ask Claude to rate its own confidence and go ahead if the rating is high
Automate the scheduling step first and then see whether the process speeds up
Check actual timings for each step, because Claude can judge only from the description it was given
questions.explanation: A bottleneck is a measurable constraint. Claude reasoned from a description that may leave out delays or exaggerate others, so timing data should confirm the diagnosis before work begins. Self-rated confidence is not evidence, and acting first and measuring later risks fixing the wrong step.

questions.question: A team is about to launch a Claude-assisted workflow and wants to anticipate what could go wrong. Which request to Claude is most useful?
options: Estimate the percentage chance that the launch will succeed, and report that number to the sponsor
Assume the launch failed six months from now and list likely causes by category, then have the team rank them and plan responses
Confirm that the plan is sound so that the team can go ahead with confidence
List the risks that earlier projects in the company recorded, and ignore anything new
questions.explanation: A pre-mortem assumes failure and works backward, which surfaces weaknesses that optimism hides. Claude can brainstorm broadly; the team ranks the causes and owns the mitigations. A success percentage has no sound basis, asking for confirmation invites agreement, and limiting the list to past risks misses new ones.

questions.question: Two software tools could support a team's reporting, and a manager wants a defensible comparison. What is the best way to involve Claude?
options: Ask which tool is better and follow its answer, since it can weigh more factors than a person can
Let Claude invent the criteria and weights, then present them to leadership as objective
Agree the criteria and weights with stakeholders, then have Claude draft a scored comparison that people check against vendor documentation
Ask Claude to summarize each vendor's marketing page and treat the stronger-sounding summary as the better tool
questions.explanation: A decision matrix is only as good as its criteria and weights, which express the organization's priorities and have to come from people. Claude can draft scores and organize evidence, and people verify it against vendor documentation. Asking for a verdict, inventing weights or comparing marketing copy skips that groundwork.

questions.question: An operations lead wants to try out an idea for a shift-coverage calculator with her team before involving IT. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Ask IT to build a production version first, so the team tests the real thing
Write a detailed specification and have the team review it for a month before building anything
Have Claude generate a spreadsheet version and roll it out to every site immediately
Ask Claude to build a working prototype as an artifact, let the team try it, and refine it from their feedback
questions.explanation: A quick prototype gives users something real to react to, which clarifies needs cheaply. IT is brought in once the idea is validated and needs company-system integration or scale. A production build or a long specification front-loads cost before learning, and an immediate roll-out skips testing.

questions.question: After a two-week pilot, users report that Claude's meeting summaries often leave out who owns each action item. What is the best response?
options: Tell users to add the missing owners by hand after each summary
Switch every user to the most capable model, since a stronger model will not leave things out
Update the template or instructions to require an owner for every action item, then rerun a set of past meetings and compare the results
Rebuild the workflow from scratch with new instructions, since the pilot has clearly failed
questions.explanation: The pilot found a specific, fixable gap. Updating the instructions and replaying past meetings shows whether the change worked without disrupting users. Manual patching leaves the cause in place, a bigger model does not guarantee following a rule that was never stated, and starting over discards what already works.

questions.question: A marketing operations specialist wants every new lead in the company's customer-management system to trigger a drafted email from Claude automatically, with nobody pasting anything. How should she proceed?
options: Describe the goal, the data involved and the volume, and take it to Claude Developers or Architects to design the integration
Connect the system herself by copying an access key into a Project's instructions so that Claude can read the leads
Ask Claude to explain how to build the integration, then deploy whatever code it produces
Paste each new lead into a chat by hand and describe the process as automated
questions.explanation: Automatic triggering from a company system is an integration with authentication, reliability and security concerns, which goes beyond Associate scope and belongs with Developers and Architects. Her contribution is a clear problem statement. Secrets never belong in instructions, unreviewed generated code should not go live, and manual pasting is not automation.

questions.question: A support team writes every customer reply from scratch, and agents lose time searching old tickets for similar cases. Refund disputes are common. What is the lowest-risk way to bring Claude into this workflow?
options: Let Claude send replies directly to customers, with agents handling only complaints
Have Claude draft replies from the ticket and a set of approved answers, with the agent editing and sending each one
Replace the ticket system with a chat in which customers discuss refunds directly with Claude
Leave the process unchanged, because customer replies are too sensitive for any AI assistance
questions.explanation: Drafting with an agent in the loop removes the search-and-write effort while a person still checks refund commitments before anything is sent. Sending directly or routing customers to Claude removes review where errors are costly, and refusing all assistance gives up a safe gain.

questions.question: A team's monthly report runs through these steps: collect figures, check them, write the narrative, review, publish. Which step is the best first integration point for Claude?
options: The review step, so that Claude approves the report instead of a manager
The publish step, so that the report goes out without waiting on anyone
The figure-checking step, with Claude's recalculations accepted as final
The narrative step, drafting text from the checked figures for a person to edit
questions.explanation: Drafting prose from verified numbers is repetitive, text-heavy and easy to review, and a manager still approves the result. Handing review or publication to Claude removes human accountability, and accepting its recalculations as final skips independent verification.

questions.question: Staff retype handwritten site-visit notes into a form, and a coordinator then rewrites them as a client summary. Which change is a redesign of the workflow, rather than just adding Claude to it?
options: Staff photograph the notes, Claude drafts the client summary directly, and the coordinator reviews it, so the retyping and rewriting steps disappear
Staff keep retyping the notes, and the coordinator asks Claude to polish the wording of the finished summary
The coordinator uses Claude to check spelling in the form after staff finish typing it
Staff retype the notes into a chat message instead of a form, and the coordinator rewrites them as before
questions.explanation: A redesign rebuilds the sequence so that Claude's strengths remove steps altogether. The other options leave the old structure intact and bolt Claude on, or swap one container for another, so the same retyping and rewriting remain.

questions.question: Three months after launch, few staff use a Claude-assisted workflow that the team built. What should the workflow owner do first?
options: Make use mandatory and track who has not logged in
Add more features, since the current ones are evidently not attractive enough
Ask users what stops them, such as trust in the output, training or extra effort, and fix the workflow or support accordingly
Wait another quarter, since adoption normally grows on its own
questions.explanation: Low use is an adoption problem, and the cause stays unknown until users are asked. Distrust, missing training and a clumsy step each need a different remedy. Mandates breed workarounds, extra features may not touch the barrier, and waiting assumes the problem will resolve itself.

questions.question: A department head wants Claude's first-draft contract summaries available to 200 staff next week. What is the most prudent rollout?
options: Launch to all 200 staff at once, so that everyone benefits and feedback arrives quickly
Run a pilot with a small team, measure accuracy and time saved, fix problems, then widen access in stages
Give access only to the most senior staff, who will not need training or guidance
Launch to all 200 staff but drop the review step, to encourage adoption
questions.explanation: A staged rollout limits the damage from early problems and produces the evidence needed to expand with confidence. Launching to everyone at once or removing review multiplies the risk, and restricting access to senior staff does nothing about training or accuracy.

questions.question: An executive asks, 'Can Claude replace our analysts?' Which answer is the most accurate and useful?
options: Yes, current models are accurate enough for analysts' work to be handed over to them entirely
No, AI output is too unreliable to be used in analysis at all
That is a question for the developers, who understand the technology better than analysts do
Claude speeds up drafting and first-pass analysis, but its output still needs checking, so the pilot data shows where it supports analysts instead
questions.explanation: A balanced answer states both the value and the limits and points to pilot evidence. Claiming replacement overstates reliability, dismissing Claude ignores real gains, and deflecting avoids the stakeholder's actual decision.

questions.question: A team lead is preparing the results slide for a six-week Claude pilot. Which set of measures will be the most credible to the finance team?
options: Time per report and rework rate before and after the pilot, plus the issues found and how they were handled
The number of prompts sent each week and the number of staff who logged in
Quotes from three enthusiastic users and the best example of Claude's output
Claude's own estimate of how much time it saved the team
questions.explanation: Credible evidence compares measured outcomes with a baseline and is candid about problems. Activity counts show use, not value; testimonials and a single best example are selective; and Claude cannot know how long the team's work really took.

questions.question: A sponsor believes Claude 'never makes mistakes' and plans to skip review in the new workflow. How should the team lead respond?
options: Agree, to avoid dampening enthusiasm, and mention limitations only if problems appear later
Explain that AI is generally unreliable and recommend not using it for any important work
Describe typical failure modes, such as inaccurate specifics and outdated information, with examples from the pilot, and show the review steps built into the workflow
Hand the sponsor a long legal disclaimer to sign and continue as planned
questions.explanation: Honest expectations backed by concrete examples keep trust when errors occur and protect the workflow's review steps. Agreeing creates false confidence, blanket negativity discards real value, and a disclaimer does not change how the output is used.

questions.question: Sales sends a business analyst a vague request: 'We need better lead tracking.' She wants to understand the underlying need before proposing anything. What should she ask Claude to do?
options: Propose three software products that would solve lead tracking
Draft interview questions about the sales team's current process, pain points and desired outcomes, and sketch a few possible use cases to test with them
Write a full specification for a lead-tracking system based on typical industry practice
Estimate a budget for a lead-tracking solution, since leadership will ask about cost first
questions.explanation: When the need is unclear, the first job is to understand it. Claude can prepare interview questions and sketch candidate use cases, but the answers must come from sales. Jumping to products, a specification or a budget builds on a guess.

questions.question: A director wants to think through options for restructuring a team. She asks Claude to propose approaches and challenge each one, going back and forth before she decides herself. Which mode of AI interaction does this describe?
options: Automation, in which Claude executes a precisely defined task and the person supplies every instruction
Agency, in which Claude is set up in advance to act on her behalf without being asked each time
Augmentation, in which she and Claude work back and forth as thinking partners while she keeps the judgment
Full delegation, in which Claude's recommendation becomes the outcome without further review
questions.explanation: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework names three modes. Working back and forth as thinking partners while the person decides is augmentation. Automation is Claude carrying out a defined task on instruction, agency is configuring Claude to act independently on future tasks, and handing the decision to Claude is not a mode at all and would remove human accountability.

questions.question: A coordinator has built a Claude-assisted weekly update that only she knows how to run. Which action best makes the workflow sustainable?
options: Write a short procedure covering the inputs, the template or instructions used, who reviews the output, where it goes and what to do if it fails
Save the best chat so far and tell colleagues to search for it whenever they need it
Leave it informal, because documentation slows down a small workflow
Ask Claude to remember the process so that any colleague can ask it to run the workflow
questions.explanation: A written procedure lets colleagues repeat the workflow and keeps it running when its builder is away. A single saved chat is a poor template, leaving it undocumented concentrates knowledge in one person, and Claude's memory is personal rather than a shared record of a team process.

questions.question: A manager is planning the move from a manual onboarding process to a Claude-assisted one and wants a gap analysis. What does Claude need from her to make the analysis useful?
options: Only a description of the target state, since Claude can infer how the current process works
A description of today's steps, owners and timings along with the target outcomes, which she then checks with the people involved
Only a description of the current process, since Claude knows what an ideal process looks like
Nothing, because Claude will fill in typical benchmarks from its own training data
questions.explanation: A gap analysis compares two states, and Claude can only compare what it has been given. Real steps, owners and timings plus clear target outcomes let it list the gaps, and the people involved confirm them. Generic benchmarks or one-sided input produce a list that may not describe this organization.

questions.question: Before presenting a proposed workflow change, a manager wants to find objections early. Which use of Claude is the most helpful?
options: Ask Claude whether anyone will object, and present the proposal only if it says no
Ask Claude to predict exactly how each executive will vote
Skip this step, because Claude has no insight into how people react to change
Ask Claude to review the proposal from the viewpoint of each affected group, such as end users, finance and security, and list likely objections, then test them with real people
questions.explanation: Claude can generate plausible objections and questions from several viewpoints, which prepares the presenter and exposes weak points. They are hypotheses to test with the real stakeholders. A yes-or-no check invites reassurance, predicting votes is guesswork, and ignoring the technique wastes a cheap rehearsal.

questions.question: A coordinator wants Claude to turn interview notes from four stakeholders into a requirements list. Which TWO additions to her request help most? (Choose two.)
options: Label whose notes are whose, so that each requirement can be traced to its source
Ask Claude to flag contradictions between stakeholders and to list any assumptions it had to make
Ask Claude to produce as many requirements as possible, so that nothing is missed
Tell Claude to resolve any conflicts itself and present only a final merged list
Remove the stakeholders' names, so that Claude is not influenced by who said what
questions.explanation: Traceability, and visible conflicts and assumptions, let people review the output efficiently and confirm it with the right stakeholder. Volume is not quality, silent conflict resolution hides decisions that belong to stakeholders, and anonymizing removes the traceability needed to check each item.

questions.question: Which THREE characteristics make a task a good first Claude pilot? (Choose three.)
options: It recurs often enough that the time savings add up
Its inputs are text and reasonably well structured
A person who knows the subject can check the output quickly
A mistake would directly affect an individual's employment or credit
It needs restricted data that policy does not allow in the tool
questions.explanation: Frequent, text-based and easily checked work shows value quickly and safely. Decisions that affect a person's job or credit are high-risk, and a task that requires data the tool is not approved for is not a pilot candidate until the data question is solved.

questions.question: Which TWO requests should be escalated to Claude Developers or Architects rather than built by an Associate alone? (Choose two.)
options: Process every incoming order email overnight and write the results straight into the company database
Connect Claude to an internal system that needs custom authentication and holds sensitive customer records
Create a Project holding the team's style guide and sample reports
Build an artifact prototype of a simple budget calculator to test with colleagues
Write a reusable prompt template for weekly status summaries
questions.explanation: Scheduled processing that writes into company systems, and integrations with authentication and sensitive records, are technical implementations beyond Associate scope. Projects, artifact prototypes and prompt templates are everyday tasks that an Associate can build and refine.

questions.question: Which THREE items belong in the written procedure for a Claude-assisted workflow? (Choose three.)
options: The inputs required and where they come from
The instructions or template used, and who maintains them
Who reviews the output, and what happens when the review fails
A transcript of every chat in which the workflow was tested
A statement promising that Claude's output will be correct
questions.explanation: A procedure that names the inputs, the instructions and owner, and the review step lets someone else run and maintain the workflow. Test transcripts are clutter, and no procedure can promise that the output will be correct, which is why the review step exists.

questions.question: Which TWO statements describe a sound value case for a Claude workflow? (Choose two.)
options: It compares measured results with a baseline recorded before the pilot
It states the known limitations and the review that stays with people
It relies on the model's own estimate of the hours saved
It leaves out costs so that the benefit looks larger
It rests on one impressive example of Claude's output
questions.explanation: A credible value case rests on measured change against a baseline and is open about limits and remaining human checks. A self-estimate, hidden costs and a cherry-picked example all weaken trust when they are noticed.

questions.question: Which TWO signs show that a process step should stay under human control rather than be handed to Claude? (Choose two.)
options: The output decides whether an individual gets a job, a loan or a benefit
A mistake would be costly or hard to reverse once it is sent
The step is repetitive and easy to check afterwards
The inputs are plain text
The step takes a lot of staff time today
questions.explanation: Decisions about individuals and errors that cannot easily be undone call for people in control, with Claude at most assisting. Repetition, text inputs and time cost are reasons to consider Claude, not reasons to keep it out.

questions.question: A requirements list that Claude drafted from interview notes still needs to be confirmed with the stakeholders who own the need.
questions.explanation: Claude can organize and probe the notes, but only the stakeholders can confirm that the list says what they need.

questions.question: In a pre-mortem, the team imagines that a project has already failed and works backward to list the reasons, and Claude can help brainstorm them.
questions.explanation: Assuming failure frees people to name weaknesses they would otherwise play down. Claude can generate causes by category, and the team ranks them and plans responses.

questions.question: In the augmentation mode of AI interaction, Claude acts as a thinking partner while the person keeps direction and judgment.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework describes augmentation as humans and AI collaborating as thinking partners, as opposed to automation, where Claude executes a defined task, and agency, where Claude acts independently on future tasks.

questions.question: Once a Claude-assisted workflow has produced good results for a week, its review steps should be removed to save time.
questions.explanation: One good week is a thin basis for removing review. Controls are relaxed in stages, only where results over a longer period justify it, and never where errors would be costly.

questions.question: Recording how long a task takes before Claude is introduced makes it possible to show later whether the workflow improved.
questions.explanation: A baseline gives the comparison that turns 'it feels faster' into evidence stakeholders can trust.

questions.question: Leaving Claude's limitations out of a stakeholder presentation is a good way to build lasting support.
questions.explanation: Support built on an overstated picture collapses at the first visible error. Presenting limits alongside benefits and controls builds credibility.

questions.question: When Claude analyzes a process from a written description, it can miss delays or problems that the description left out.
questions.explanation: Claude works from what it has been told. Timing data and conversations with the people who do the work fill the gaps.

questions.question: Associates are expected to design enterprise-scale integrations and custom connectors on their own.
questions.explanation: The exam guide places enterprise-scale designs and technical integrations with Claude Architects and Developers, to whom Associates escalate more complex work.

questions.question: A quick prototype built as an artifact can help a team learn what users need before a full solution is built.
questions.explanation: Putting something real in front of users surfaces needs and objections cheaply, before anyone commits to a larger build.

questions.question: Piloting a new Claude workflow with a small group first reduces the risk of spreading early problems.
questions.explanation: A pilot limits the damage from early flaws and produces measured results that justify wider rollout.

questions.question: A decision matrix is trustworthy only when Claude, not the stakeholders, sets the weights for the criteria.
questions.explanation: Weights express the organization's priorities, so stakeholders must set them. Claude can suggest criteria and draft scores that people then check.

questions.question: A customer-care lead is setting up a Project for her agents. She has a 20-page refund policy, and she wants every draft reply to open with an apology, stay under 150 words and quote the policy section it relies on. How should she set it up?
options: Paste the refund policy and the three drafting rules together into the project instructions, so that everything Claude needs is in one place
Upload the refund policy as project knowledge and write the three drafting rules into the project description, where the whole team can read them
Upload the refund policy as project knowledge and write the three drafting rules into the project instructions
Upload the refund policy as project knowledge and ask each agent to type the three drafting rules at the start of every new chat
questions.explanation: Rules about how to draft belong in the project instructions, which apply to every chat in the Project, while the policy is reference material that belongs in project knowledge. Merging both into the instructions mixes facts with rules and makes the policy hard to update. Claude cannot see a Project's description, so rules placed there are never applied. Retyping the rules in every chat is exactly what standing instructions are meant to avoid, and it invites drift between agents.

questions.question: An HR specialist types 'Always cite the policy section and never promise exceptions' into the description field of her new Project. Claude's replies ignore the rule. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: Claude cannot see a Project's name or description, so the rule belongs in the project instructions
Claude cannot see the description, so she should repeat the rule at the start of every chat in the Project
Claude reads the description only after the Project is shared with colleagues, so she should invite one to unlock it
The rule needs its reasons spelled out, so she should extend the description with a paragraph on why exceptions are risky
questions.explanation: The Help Center states that Claude has no access to a Project's name and description; they are labels for people. Standing rules go in the project instructions, which apply to every chat in the Project. Repeating the rule in each chat has the right diagnosis but depends on every user remembering it. Sharing the Project changes who can see it, not what Claude reads, and giving reasons helps Claude apply a rule only when Claude can see the rule in the first place.

questions.question: In one chat inside a team's Project, an analyst tells Claude to report revenue in thousands of euros. In a new chat in the same Project the next day, Claude reports in plain euros. What is the most reliable way to make the preference apply to everyone who uses the Project?
options: Ask Claude at the end of each chat to remember the preference for the next chat in the Project
Ask each analyst to add the preference to their own account-wide instructions as a standing rule
Continue all revenue analysis in the original chat so that the preference stays in view
Add the preference to the project instructions so that every chat in the Project applies it
questions.explanation: Context from one chat is not shared with the other chats in a Project unless it is added to the Project's knowledge or instructions, so a standing rule belongs in the project instructions. Asking Claude to remember is personal and unreliable rather than a shared configuration. Account-wide instructions would apply to all of that analyst's conversations, including unrelated work, and depend on every person doing it. One endless chat grows unwieldy and leaves everyone else out.

questions.question: A freelance consultant works for two clients. Client A wants formal British English; Client B wants a casual American tone. She also wants every answer, for either client, to define acronyms on first use. Where should she save these rules?
options: Each client's style rules in that client's own Project, and the acronym rule in her account-wide instructions
All three rules in her account-wide instructions, each labeled with the client it applies to
Both clients' style rules in one Project, with a line telling Claude which client is being discussed
All three rules as documents in a single Project's knowledge, so that Claude can look up whichever one applies
questions.explanation: Account-wide instructions apply to every conversation, so they suit only preferences that hold everywhere, such as defining acronyms. Client-specific rules belong in that client's Project, whose instructions apply to its chats alone. Putting conflicting style rules in one place makes Claude guess which applies and lets one client's tone leak into the other's work. Instructions describe behavior while knowledge is reference material, so rules saved as documents are not applied as standing instructions.

questions.question: A policy team's Project now holds several hundred documents, and an indicator shows that Claude is searching the material rather than reading all of it at once. Answers sometimes draw on the wrong policy. Which habit helps most?
options: Combine all of the documents into one large file so that Claude has a single document to search
Copy the most important policies into the project instructions so that they are always in view
Name the specific document in each question, and keep clear, descriptive file names
Ask Claude to read every file in full before it answers each question
questions.explanation: When knowledge is large, retrieval pulls out the passages that matter instead of loading everything, so precise pointers steer it best: naming the document and using descriptive file names. One merged file removes the structure that tells one policy from another. Copying policies into the instructions creates second copies that go stale and crowds the standing context. Reading every file in full is the opposite of how retrieval handles volume.

questions.question: A benefits Project still contains last year's leave policy alongside the updated policy that was added in the spring. Staff report that Claude sometimes quotes the old entitlements. What is the best fix?
options: Add an instruction telling Claude to prefer the most recent information whenever documents disagree
Put the word 'OLD' at the start of the previous policy's file name and leave it in the Project
Ask staff to compare any entitlement Claude quotes with the current policy before relying on it
Remove the outdated policy so that the Project holds one current, clearly named version
questions.explanation: A Project keeps whatever it is given and Claude cannot tell by itself that a file is outdated, so the reliable fix is a single source of truth. An instruction to prefer newer information depends on Claude judging which document is newer and leaves two conflicting copies in place. A renamed file can still be retrieved and quoted. Asking staff to double-check treats the symptom and puts the burden on every user.

questions.question: An analyst who uses the Google Drive connector asks Claude to summarize the 'Q3 board pack' folder. Claude cannot find it, although a colleague can open the folder. What is the best first step?
options: Ask an administrator to give Claude its own account with access to the folder
Check whether her own Google account has been given access to that folder
Ask the colleague to export the folder's documents and upload them to the chat
Disconnect and reconnect the connector until the folder appears
questions.explanation: Claude inherits the signed-in person's permissions, so it can see only what her own account can open. If a colleague can see the folder and she cannot, the gap is probably her access, which the folder's owner or an administrator can fix. Claude has no separate account to authorize. Passing files around by hand works around the missing permission instead of resolving it and may sidestep the access decision the owner made. Reconnecting does not change what her account is allowed to open.

questions.question: An Owner on a Team plan enables the Google Drive connector for the whole organization. A week later, several members say that Claude still cannot see any of their documents. What is the most likely reason?
options: Claude needs several days to process the organization's files after enablement, so members should simply wait
The Owner must first copy each member's documents into a shared Project before they can be read
Enabling made the connector available, but each member still has to sign in to Google with their own account
Only Owners can use connectors, so members must be promoted before they can connect their accounts
questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, enablement makes a connector available to the organization but grants nobody access to data. Each person normally authenticates individually, which keeps Claude within that person's own permissions. Waiting changes nothing because no step is pending, no copying into Projects is involved, and members do not need the Owner role to connect their own accounts.

questions.question: An Owner wants staff to let Claude search and read documents in a connected service freely, but wants any change or deletion to need a person's confirmation. What should the Owner do?
options: Block the connector for everyone and ask staff to upload the files they need into their chats instead
Allow every action on the connector and train staff to watch closely for unwanted changes
Replace individual sign-in with one shared read-only login so that nobody can change anything
Let reading actions run without asking, and set writing and deleting actions to need approval
questions.explanation: Owners can set a connector's actions to run freely, need approval or be blocked, and these settings only narrow what the service already permits. Blocking everything throws away the live access that makes the connector useful. Allowing everything and relying on vigilance replaces a configured control with hope. A shared login removes the link to each person's own permissions and can reach whatever that credential can, which widens exposure instead of limiting it.

questions.question: A team member finds a custom connector on a public forum that promises to link Claude to the company's project-tracking tool. She is tempted to add it, reasoning that a connector can only see what she can already open. What is the best course of action?
options: Add it to a private Project first, since a Project keeps any problems contained to that workspace
Ask the Owner or IT to review the source first, since Anthropic does not verify custom connectors
Add it, since a connector can only see what she can already open and the risk is therefore removed
Add it for now and remove it later if the team does not find it useful or runs into trouble
questions.explanation: Anthropic does not verify custom connectors, and the connected service handles data under its own terms, so trust in the publisher has to be checked before anything is connected. Permission inheritance limits what Claude can reach for a person, but an unknown party's connector still handles the data it touches, and one built on a shared credential reaches whatever that credential allows. Making a Project private changes who sees the Project, not what a connector can do, and trying it first exposes data in the meantime.

questions.question: A procurement team is writing the standing, system-level instructions for a Project that drafts replies to supplier queries. Which approach is most likely to give consistent, useful replies?
options: Describe Claude as a world-class procurement expert and tell it to be thorough, accurate and professional in every reply, whatever the question
Paste the entire supplier handbook into the instructions so that the rules and the facts they rely on sit together in one place
Name the reader and the tone, set a length and layout, point to the file to quote, and say what to do when the answer is missing
Write short commands in capital letters, such as NEVER GUESS and ALWAYS BE ACCURATE, so that no rule can be overlooked
questions.explanation: Effective standing instructions are specific: the audience and tone, the format, the source to rely on and a fallback for missing information. A grand title and general virtues give Claude nothing to act on. The handbook is reference material that belongs in knowledge, where it can be updated without touching the rules. Anthropic's guidance for current models is to use normal, clear wording rather than shouted commands, which can lead Claude to over-apply a rule.

questions.question: A legal-operations Project answers staff questions from an uploaded contract playbook. Now and then Claude gives confident guidance on a question that the playbook does not cover. Which change to the instructions best reduces this?
options: Tell Claude to answer only from the playbook, cite the section it used, and say when the playbook is silent and who to ask
Tell Claude to be extra careful and to double-check every answer before it replies to a staff member
Tell Claude to refuse any question whose topic is not listed in the playbook's table of contents
Add the most common out-of-scope questions, with model answers written by the team, to the instructions
questions.explanation: A fallback instruction removes the pressure to fill gaps with plausible guesses: it grounds answers in the supplied document, asks for the source, and says what to do when the document does not answer, such as route the question to a named person. 'Be careful' gives Claude nothing concrete to do. Refusing by table of contents blocks questions that the body of the playbook does answer. A growing list of model answers chases examples instead of fixing the rule, and it goes stale.

questions.question: The instructions of a shared reporting Project have grown to forty rules added by different people over a year. They include 'keep every answer under 100 words' and 'always give a full step-by-step explanation'. Replies are now erratic. What is the best fix?
options: Add a final rule saying that the most recent rule wins whenever two rules in the list disagree with each other
Review the whole set, merge duplicates, resolve conflicts and explain the reason for each remaining rule
Put the most important rules in capital letters so that they outweigh the others in the list
Delete the instructions entirely and rely on the uploaded files to guide how Claude replies
questions.explanation: Rules that pull in opposite directions leave Claude to guess, so the cure is to edit the set into one consistent, explained list and then test it. A 'latest rule wins' line assumes Claude can tell which rule is latest, and capitals add pressure without resolving the contradiction. Deleting everything throws away the rules that were working, and uploaded files supply facts, not behavior.

questions.question: A communications team's Project instructions include this month's product prices and promotion end dates, so someone has to rewrite the instructions every month, and an old figure occasionally survives. What is the better design?
options: Keep the figures in the instructions but have Claude ask for the current prices at the start of each chat
Move the figures into a named knowledge file that is replaced each month, and have the instructions say to quote it
Move the prices and dates into the account-wide instructions, since they are needed in every conversation
Remove the figures from the Project altogether and ask each writer to paste the current ones into every request
questions.explanation: Instructions should hold stable behavior; facts that change belong in one knowledge file that can be swapped without touching the rules, with the instructions telling Claude to quote it. Having Claude ask for prices or having writers paste them reintroduces manual steps and errors. Account-wide instructions would push this month's promotions into every unrelated conversation.

questions.question: The owner of a shared Project wants to change its instructions to fix a tone problem. How should she make the change so that she does not break behavior that works today?
options: Make the change in the live Project, then watch for complaints over the next week
Make this change together with the other improvements she has in mind, to save the team repeated updates
Ask Claude whether the new instructions look better and keep them if it agrees
Run a small fixed set of representative requests before and after the change, and compare the results
questions.explanation: A regression test set shows whether the change fixed the tone and whether anything else got worse, because the same requests, including a few tricky ones, are used each time. Waiting for complaints makes the users the test. Bundling several changes hides which one caused a problem. Claude's opinion of its own instructions is not evidence of how the outputs actually change.

questions.question: Thirty people share a Project. Several of them add their own files and adjust the instructions, and answers have become inconsistent. What should the Project's owner do?
options: Post a message asking everyone to stop editing the Project, and trust the team to follow it
Let everyone keep editing but ask them to leave a note in the chat explaining each change they make
Delete the shared Project and have each person maintain a private Project of their own instead
Limit edit rights to a few named maintainers and give everyone else access to view and chat
questions.explanation: Sharing offers Can view and Can edit roles, so a configuration can be protected by permissions rather than by good intentions: only maintainers who understand the Project's purpose change its instructions and files. A request to stop relies on compliance. Notes in chats are scattered and do not prevent a bad edit. Personal Projects multiply the versions, so each person's answers drift further apart.

questions.question: After a policy update, a Project owner replaced two knowledge files and rewrote part of the instructions. Two days later, staff complain that answers have 'changed without warning', and nobody can say what was altered. What would have prevented this?
options: Keeping a change log of what was changed, by whom and why, and telling users about the update
Making all edits outside working hours so that fewer people notice a difference in the answers
Telling Claude to announce at the start of each chat that the Project's settings have been updated
Holding policy updates until the next quarterly review so that changes arrive in one batch
questions.explanation: A change log records what changed so that a shift in behavior can be traced and reversed, and a short notice tells users what to expect. Editing in quiet hours hides the change instead of explaining it. Claude has no way of knowing what was edited, so an announcement instruction cannot work. Holding a policy update for a quarter leaves stale knowledge in use.

questions.question: A team installed a custom skill for formatting expense summaries, but Claude rarely uses it when someone asks for an expense summary. What is the best first fix?
options: Paste the skill's full instructions into every expense request so that Claude always sees them
Rewrite the skill's description to say what it does and when to use it, then retest it with sample requests
Add more reference files to the skill so that it looks more substantial and complete to Claude
Move the skill's instructions into the account-wide instructions so they apply to every conversation
questions.explanation: Claude first sees only a skill's name and description and decides from them whether to load the rest, so a vague description means the skill is ignored or fires at the wrong time. Sharpening it and retesting with sample requests fixes the cause. Pasting the instructions defeats the purpose of a skill, extra files do not change how a skill is selected, and account-wide instructions would apply the formatting to every conversation, expenses or not.

questions.question: A colleague forwards a skill file from a public website that promises to 'polish any report automatically'. It includes scripts. What should happen before anyone installs it?
options: Install it in a personal account first, since a skill can only change how a report looks and cannot reach anything else
Install it and try it on non-sensitive documents only, which removes any risk from an unknown publisher
Have someone who manages the organization's tools review the publisher and scripts first, and add it only if trusted
Install it for the whole team at once so that any problems show up quickly and can be fixed together
questions.explanation: A skill can carry instructions and code, and the Help Center warns that untrusted skills can expose data through prompt injection or data exfiltration, so skills should come only from trusted sources and be reviewed first. A skill is not limited to appearance. Test data limits the damage but does not make an unknown publisher trustworthy, and rolling it out to everyone multiplies the exposure.

questions.question: A support team is dividing its material between a Project's instructions and its knowledge. Which TWO items belong in the instructions? (Choose two.)
options: Who will read the replies and the tone they should have
The full text of the current returns policy
What Claude should do when the knowledge does not contain the answer
Last quarter's customer-satisfaction survey results
The product catalogue with this month's prices
questions.explanation: Instructions hold standing guidance about behavior: the audience and tone, and a fallback for questions the knowledge cannot answer. The returns policy, the survey results and the price list are reference material, which belongs in project knowledge, where it can be replaced when it changes without touching the rules.

questions.question: A shared Project's knowledge has become unreliable because old and new documents are mixed together. Which THREE practices keep uploaded knowledge trustworthy? (Choose three.)
options: Upload every draft as well, in case someone wants to compare versions
Keep one approved version of each document and retire superseded copies
Rely on Claude to notice which documents are out of date and ignore them
Give each file a descriptive name that includes its date or version
Review the files on a schedule and replace any that no longer match current policy
questions.explanation: A single source of truth, descriptive names with dates or versions, and a regular review keep a Project current and let both people and retrieval pick the right file. Extra drafts add conflicting copies, and Claude cannot reliably tell that a file is outdated: it quotes what it is given.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about connecting Claude to services such as Google Drive and Gmail are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Claude can reach only the files and messages that the signed-in person could already open
An Owner's permission settings can give Claude more access than the connected service itself allows
On a Team plan, once an Owner enables a connector, each person still signs in with their own account
Claude reads charts and pictures embedded in a Google Doc in the same way as the text
Enabling a connector lets Claude search every employee's mailbox for the Owner
questions.explanation: Claude inherits each person's own permissions, and on Team and Enterprise plans enablement makes a connector available without granting access, so members normally authenticate individually. Owner settings can only narrow what a service allows, never widen it. The Drive connector reads text only, so images inside documents are not seen, and the Gmail connector works within the mail the connected person can already open.

questions.question: The owner of a shared Project has just edited its instructions. Which TWO steps best protect the people who rely on it? (Choose two.)
options: Rerun a fixed set of representative requests and compare the answers with notes on what good looks like
Delete the old chats so that nobody sees answers produced under the earlier instructions
Ask Claude to confirm that the new instructions are an improvement
Record what changed, who changed it and why, and tell users what is different
Wait for users to report problems before checking anything
questions.explanation: Rerunning the same test requests shows whether anything got worse, and a change log plus a short notice lets users and colleagues trace and understand shifts in behavior. Deleting chats hides evidence without fixing anything, Claude's agreement is not a measurement of output quality, and waiting for complaints turns users into testers.

questions.question: Which TWO situations call for building a skill rather than adding more text to a Project's instructions? (Choose two.)
options: A fixed report layout must be applied across many chats and Projects, but only when someone asks for that report
The team's current price list must be available to every chat in one shared Project, whoever starts it
A procedure with a template file and a script should be loaded only when a matching request comes up
A personal preference for British spelling should apply to every conversation the person has
A reminder that this quarter's priority is the product launch should shape every reply in one Project
questions.explanation: A skill packages a procedure that Claude loads on demand when a request matches, and it works across chats and Projects, which fits a recurring report layout and a procedure with its own template and script. A price list is project knowledge, a preference for every conversation is an account-wide instruction, and a standing priority for one Project's replies is a project instruction.

questions.question: Claude can read a Project's name and description, so standing rules can safely be written in the description field.
questions.explanation: The Help Center says Claude does not have access to a Project's name or description; they are labels for people. Standing rules belong in the project instructions.

questions.question: Instructions saved in a Project apply to every chat inside that Project, but not to the person's chats outside it.
questions.explanation: Project instructions are scoped to their own Project. The account-wide setting is the one that follows a person into every conversation.

questions.question: An Owner's permission settings on a connector can give Claude more access than the connected service itself allows.
questions.explanation: Owner settings such as always allow, needs approval and blocked only narrow what the source system already permits. They never grant more access than the service gives.

questions.question: With the Gmail connector, Claude works only within the mail that the connected person can already open.
questions.explanation: Claude inherits the signed-in person's permissions in the connected service, so it cannot see other people's mailboxes. When something cannot be found, the first check is the person's own access.

questions.question: A Google Doc added to a Project from Drive stays linked to the live document, whereas a file uploaded from a computer remains a static copy.
questions.explanation: Docs added from Drive stay in step with the source, so Claude works from the current version. An uploaded file changes only when someone replaces it, which is why uploads of frequently changing documents go stale.

questions.question: Telling Claude what to do when the knowledge does not contain an answer, for example to say so and name who to ask, reduces confident guessing.
questions.explanation: A fallback instruction gives Claude a sanctioned alternative to inventing a plausible answer, and it works best when paired with a rule to quote the source whenever an answer does exist.

questions.question: An instruction telling Claude to ignore an old policy file is just as reliable as removing that file from the Project.
questions.explanation: The file stays available and can still be retrieved and quoted. Instructions guide behavior but do not guarantee a document is never used, whereas removing the file leaves a single source of truth.

questions.question: Claude loads the full contents of every installed skill at the start of each conversation.
questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: Claude first sees only each skill's name and description and reads the rest only when a request matches, which stops many skills from crowding the context window.

questions.question: An HR coordinator proposes having Claude score every incoming application and automatically reject anyone below a cutoff, so recruiters only see the top candidates. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Approve it, because applying the same standard to every application is fair by design and removes recruiter inconsistency
Approve it only for scores far below the cutoff, where the risk of wrongly rejecting a strong candidate is small
Use Claude to summarize applications, with a recruiter deciding each outcome and applicants told that AI is involved
Prohibit all use of Claude anywhere in hiring, including drafting job adverts and interview questions for recruiters
questions.explanation: Hiring is a high-risk area because the output would decide about individuals. Anthropic's Usage Policy asks for a qualified person who can change the outcome to review such recommendations, and for the affected people to be told that AI was used. Claude can still summarize and organize applications. A consistent standard is not the same as a fair one, since a scoring rule can carry hidden bias; limiting automation to low scorers still rejects people without review; and banning every use gives up low-risk help such as drafting job adverts.

questions.question: A payroll specialist asks Claude whether freelance designers can be treated as independent contractors, and Claude gives a confident, detailed answer. She plans to apply it to every freelancer in the company. What is the best way to proceed?
options: Use it to prepare questions, then have HR or legal confirm the classification before it is applied
Apply the answer to all freelancers, since the reasoning was detailed and the question was a general one
Ask Claude to repeat the analysis three times and apply whichever conclusion comes up most often
Ask Claude to cite the relevant law, and apply the answer once the citation looks plausible and complete
questions.explanation: Worker classification is a legal question where a mistake affects people's rights and the company's exposure. Claude can explain the concepts and help prepare questions, but a qualified person makes the call. Detail and confidence are not credentials, agreement across repeated runs shows consistency rather than correctness, and a plausible-looking citation can still be invented, so it has to be checked against the real text by someone competent to read it.

questions.question: Two weeks before a product launch, a marketing lead asks Claude to write thirty five-star customer reviews 'in different voices' to publish on the product page. What is the best response?
options: Generate them, provided that every claim in them matches the product specification and none overstates it
Generate them, but publish them under the names of colleagues who have genuinely tried the product
Generate them, and label the section 'sample content' in small print at the bottom of the page
Decline to invent reviews; use Claude to draft requests for real customer feedback instead
questions.explanation: A review is supposed to be a real customer's opinion. Inventing reviews, or attributing them to people who did not write them, is deceptive content, which Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits (fake reviews and astroturfing) and which most company policies forbid even when every claim is accurate. Claude can legitimately help gather and summarize genuine feedback. Small print does not make a fabricated review honest.

questions.question: A customer-service lead is writing requirements for a website chat assistant that developers will build on Claude. To make it feel personal, she wants it to introduce itself as a human agent named Maya. What is the best guidance?
options: Proceed, because the answers will be accurate and customers get the help they need either way
Keep the friendly name, but have the assistant say at the start that it is an AI assistant
Proceed, but have the assistant admit to being an AI only when a customer asks directly
Proceed, and mention the use of AI in the terms of service rather than in the chat itself
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy requires consumer-facing chatbots to tell users that they are talking to AI. A name and a warm tone are fine; pretending to be a person is deception, however accurate the answers are. Admitting it only when asked still misleads everyone who does not ask, and a note buried in the terms is not a clear notice at the point of conversation.

questions.question: An HR team lists four ideas for Claude and wants to start with the one that carries the least governance risk. Which should it pick?
options: Scoring employees to decide who receives a promotion
Drafting a first version of the monthly staff newsletter for an editor to revise
Choosing which applicants are invited to interview, with no recruiter review
Writing the final message to an employee whose leave request is declined, sent without review
questions.explanation: Drafting internal content that a person edits is an assistive use: Claude supports someone's own work and an imperfect draft does little harm. The other ideas move from informing a person to deciding about one (promotion, hiring, leave) or to communicating a decision with no review. Those are the high-risk uses that call for qualified human review and notice to the people affected.

questions.question: A recruiter wants Claude to read candidates' public social-media posts and infer their religion, health conditions and family plans, in order to predict who will stay with the company. How should she proceed?
options: Go ahead, because the posts are public and Claude would only analyze what candidates chose to share
Go ahead after removing the candidates' names from the posts, which makes the analysis anonymous
Go ahead, but ask Claude to describe the traits indirectly instead of naming the characteristics
Do not do it: inferring protected characteristics for hiring is discriminatory; use job-related criteria
questions.explanation: Using protected attributes, or inferences about them, to screen candidates is discrimination, which Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits and employment law restricts. That the posts are public does not change this, removing names does not remove the characteristics, and describing them indirectly produces the same proxy. Documented, job-related criteria assessed by people, with Claude helping to summarize the evidence, are the appropriate route.

questions.question: An HR analyst wants to find which departments have the highest overtime. The export she was given has names, home addresses, national ID numbers, department and weekly hours for 4,000 staff, and company policy restricts personal data in AI tools. What is the best approach?
options: Upload only the department and weekly-hours columns, since the question needs nothing that identifies a person
Upload the full export to a Project and ask Claude not to mention any names or addresses in its analysis
Replace the names with nicknames and upload the rest, so that Claude can still check individual rows by address
Paste the export into a personal account, where the company's restrictions on personal data do not reach
questions.explanation: Data minimization means giving Claude only what the task needs. Department and hours answer the question, so the identifying columns never have to leave the file. Asking Claude not to mention names does not stop the data being shared, nicknames leave addresses and ID numbers in place, and a personal account is outside the approved tools, so using it moves the problem instead of solving it.

questions.question: A coordinator replaced customer names with 'Customer A', 'Customer B' and so on in the body of a Word report. Before uploading it to Claude under a policy that bars customer identities, which check matters most?
options: Confirm the report is within the upload size limit so that the upload does not fail halfway through
Convert the report to PDF, which removes comments, tracked changes and anything else hidden in the Word file
Look for names left in the file name, headers, comments, tracked changes and document properties
Upload it and ask Claude to confirm that the document contains no customer names or other identities
questions.explanation: Redaction is only as good as its coverage. Identifiers hide in places that are easy to forget, such as the file name, headers, comments, tracked changes and properties, so these are checked before the file leaves your control. A size check addresses a different problem, converting the format does not by itself remove identifiers, and uploading the file to ask Claude is circular because the data would already have been shared.

questions.question: A consultant is up against a deadline. Her firm's approved Claude workspace has a queue for new access requests, while her personal Claude account is available immediately. She wants to paste a client's unreleased deal terms into the personal account. What is the best course?
options: Use the personal account after switching off its model-improvement setting so that nothing is used for training
Use the personal account in an incognito chat, so that nothing is saved to her history or memory
Use the personal account but replace the client's name with 'Client X' throughout the terms
Ask her manager or IT to expedite approved access, and keep the terms out of her personal account
questions.explanation: Unreleased deal terms are confidential business information, and company data belongs in the approved tool. Privacy settings on a personal account, including incognito mode and the model-improvement toggle, do not turn it into an approved tool, and the terms can identify the deal even without the client's name. Convenience is how shadow AI starts; the compliant route is to ask for access or an exception.

questions.question: A clinic's office manager wants Claude to summarize patient intake notes so that scheduling is faster. Staff would use their own individual Claude accounts, and the clinic has no agreement with Anthropic. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Begin now, after deleting the patients' names from every note, since the remaining details are not identifying
Raise it first with the clinic's privacy or compliance officer, since patient data needs a covered service
Begin now, because the summaries stay inside the clinic and are used only for scheduling, never shared
Begin now, after getting each patient's verbal agreement to an AI assistant helping with their notes
questions.explanation: Patient notes are protected health information. In the United States a healthcare organization needs a business associate agreement, and a covered configuration, before a vendor handles it; Anthropic offers that agreement for HIPAA-ready commercial services, not for individual consumer plans. Removing names does not de-identify notes that still hold dates, places and details; internal use is still use; and informal consent does not replace the required agreement and safeguards. The privacy officer decides the compliant route.

questions.question: A team lead tells her staff, 'Our company uses a Claude Team plan, and those plans don't train on our chats by default, so you can paste anything into it.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Team plans do train on chats by default, so her statement is simply wrong about how the plan works
Commercial terms apply only to API customers, so Team plan users are treated like individual users
The training default covers Anthropic's use of data; it does not decide what company rules allow staff to paste
A provider that does not train on chats does not keep them either, so only the wording of the contract needs checking
questions.explanation: By default, Anthropic's commercial products (Team, Enterprise and the API) do not use inputs and outputs for model training, so her premise is true. But what the vendor does with data is a different question from what the company allows staff to share. Data classification, client contracts and regulation still decide what may be pasted. The other statements are factually wrong: commercial terms are not limited to the API, and data is retained for a period regardless of training.

questions.question: A colleague wants to put the shared login for the finance portal into a Project's instructions so that Claude can sign in and pull reports automatically. What is the best advice?
options: Keep credentials out of prompts, instructions and files; use an approved authenticated connection instead
That is acceptable as long as the Project is kept private to the finance team and its members are trusted
Put the password in a knowledge file instead of the instructions, where it is less visible to casual readers
Split the password across two knowledge files so that neither file reveals it on its own to a reader
questions.explanation: Passwords, keys and tokens do not belong in prompts, Project instructions or knowledge files, where they are stored as plain text, visible to everyone with access to the Project and easy to copy elsewhere. Anthropic's skills guidance likewise warns against hard-coding keys or passwords. A private Project, a different file, or a split password all still leave the secret in text that Claude and Project members can read. Properly authenticated connections or a person doing the sign-in avoid storing it.

questions.question: An employee realizes he pasted a spreadsheet of client account numbers into a personal Claude account, against company policy. He is tempted to delete the chat and say nothing. What should he do?
options: Report it promptly through the escalation path, so that security and privacy can contain it
Delete the chat and carry on with the work, since deleting a chat removes the data everywhere at once
Ask Claude to forget the spreadsheet and confirm that it has done so, then continue in the same chat
Wait a week to see whether anyone notices the mistake, and report it only if someone does
questions.explanation: A data mistake reported the same day is far easier to contain. Deleting a chat removes it from your history immediately, but deletion from back-end storage follows later, and Claude has no 'forget' control that undoes a disclosure. Staying silent leaves the company unable to assess its obligations, which may include informing clients or regulators. The escalation path exists for exactly this situation.

questions.question: While Claude reads a supplier's web page for an analyst, it suddenly starts searching her connected Drive and asks her to approve sending a file to an address outside the company. She never requested this. What should she do?
options: Approve the action, since Claude would not ask unless it had a good reason to
Ask Claude to explain, and approve the action if the explanation sounds reasonable
Stop the task, decline the action, and report the page as a possible prompt injection
Let the task finish, then delete the chat to remove the file from the conversation
questions.explanation: Web pages and files can contain hidden instructions written to hijack Claude, called prompt injection. Anthropic's guidance warns that Claude can be tricked into sending information from its context and tells people to watch for unexpected behavior and stop it. She never asked for the search or the transfer, so she should stop, decline, and tell the people responsible for security. An explanation produced by a hijacked session is not a safeguard, and deleting the chat afterwards cannot recall anything already sent.

questions.question: A project lead wants to show a colleague in another department how she built a client analysis in Claude, and plans to post the chat's share link in a team channel. What should she do first?
options: Post the link first and ask readers to report anything confidential that they happen to notice
Read the whole conversation for client details first, because everyone who opens the link sees all of it
Ask Claude to hide the sensitive parts of the conversation from anyone who opens the shared link
Share the link, since it shows only the finished analysis and not the messages that led up to it
questions.explanation: A chat share link is a snapshot of the conversation as it stood when shared, so readers see everything said in it, including client details; on Team and Enterprise plans it works only for members of the organization. She should review the text first and can unshare later to revoke the link. Posting first and asking readers to report problems exposes the content before anyone has checked it; Claude cannot selectively hide parts of a shared conversation; and the link does not show only the most recent reply.

questions.question: A communications manager wants to record internal meetings and have Claude transcribe and summarize them. Her company's AI policy lists approved tools and covers customer data but says nothing about meeting recordings. What should she do?
options: Go ahead, because the policy forbids only the things it names and recordings are not among them
Go ahead, but only with meetings that she personally judges to be non-sensitive and low in risk
Use a personal account for the transcripts, since the policy does not mention meeting recordings at all
Ask the policy owner, such as IT or compliance, before starting, and stay within approved tools meanwhile
questions.explanation: When policy is silent, the answer is to ask, not to assume permission. Recordings can contain personal data, confidential discussions and consent obligations, and only the policy owner can say how the policy applies. Judging sensitivity alone, or moving to a personal account, bypasses the people accountable for the answer.

questions.question: A team finds a third-party plugin that connects Claude to its project-management tool. A teammate suggests trying it on a live project with real data first and requesting a formal review only if it proves useful. What is the best approach?
options: Try it on live data first, since a review is worth the effort only for tools that prove useful
Request the vendor risk assessment first, and test only with non-sensitive sample data until approved
Install it under a personal account so that the company workspace is not affected by the trial
Install it, relying on its popularity with other companies as proof that it is safe to use
questions.explanation: A plugin or connector can reach company data and may be maintained by a third party. A vendor risk assessment of security, privacy and terms belongs before real data is exposed, not after; sample data lets the team judge usefulness in the meantime. A personal account is shadow AI, and popularity is not a review of your own risks. Anthropic's guidance is to install plugins and skills only from sources you trust.

questions.question: Anthropic's Usage Policy permits a certain internal use of Claude, but the company's own AI acceptable use policy forbids it. An employee asks which rule governs her work. What is the right answer?
options: The company's policy, because an employer may be stricter with its staff than the vendor is
The Usage Policy, because the vendor sets the rules for its own product and customers must follow them
Whichever of the two is more permissive, since a use that either one allows is acceptable
Neither, because she may decide for herself whether to proceed when the risk seems low to her
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy sets the outer limit for everyone, but an employer can be stricter for its own staff, for example because of client contracts or regulation, and employees follow the stricter rule. Being allowed by the vendor does not make a use allowed by your employer, and the more permissive choice is never the safe one.

questions.question: Months from now, a bank's compliance team may need to explain how an AI-assisted credit memo was prepared. Which habit best supports that?
options: Save every chat in a personal account, so that the history is available if anyone asks about it later
Rely on Claude's memory feature to recall how it helped with the memo when the question comes up
Ask Claude, when the question arises, to write down how it contributed to the memo months earlier
Keep a short record of the tool and account used, the date, the purpose, the reviewer and the edits made
