questions.explanation: An audit trail is a record the organization controls of how AI contributed and who took responsibility: tool, account, date, purpose, reviewer and edits. A personal account's chat history is not an organizational record, Claude's memory stores notes about a person's work rather than a log, and a later account from Claude would be a reconstruction of events it cannot reliably recall.

questions.question: A consultant keeps files for several clients in one shared Project. A draft report for Client A includes figures that belong to Client B. What is the best response?
options: Delete the other client's figures from the draft and send it on time, since the error has been fixed
Add an instruction to the Project telling Claude to keep each client's data apart, then carry on
Hold the report, raise it through the escalation path, and give each client a separate Project with its own access
Ask Claude to promise that it will not mix up clients in any future drafts, and keep the Project as it is
questions.explanation: The mix-up shows that one client's confidential data was available where it should not have been, which is both a possible incident to report and a design problem to fix. Least privilege means separating clients by Project and access, not asking the model to keep them apart. Deleting the figures hides the symptom, an instruction relies on wording where an access boundary is needed, and a promise from Claude is not a control.

questions.question: After three months of using Claude to shortlist applicants, an HR team notices that far fewer applicants over fifty reach the shortlist than before. The criteria given to Claude include 'recent graduates' fluency with new technology'. What is the best response?
options: Keep the process unchanged, since the criteria never mention age and so cannot be discriminatory
Add an instruction asking Claude to be unbiased and to treat all age groups fairly in the next round
Pause the shortlisting, compare outcomes by group and review the criteria with HR and legal
Remove birth dates from the applications and continue, since that settles the issue of age bias
questions.explanation: A rule that looks neutral can still disadvantage a protected group (disparate impact), and a phrase such as 'recent graduates' acts as a proxy for age. The response is to measure outcomes by group, fix the criteria with HR and legal input, and keep human accountability. The absence of the word 'age' proves nothing, an instruction to be unbiased does not change the criteria, and removing birth dates leaves proxies such as graduation years in place.

questions.question: A loan team uses Claude to draft decision summaries. Reviewers get about ten seconds per case, see only the AI's summary, and cannot change the recommendation. Which change would make the review meaningful?
options: Add a second Claude chat that rechecks the summaries written by the first one, before review
Ask reviewers to confirm each approval with a second click, so that every approval is recorded
Raise the number of cases each reviewer handles per hour so that the backlog shrinks
Give reviewers the time, the source files and the authority to override a recommendation
questions.explanation: Meaningful human review needs a qualified person with the time, the information and the authority to change the outcome; otherwise the human is a rubber stamp and automation bias takes over. A second AI check is not independent human judgment, an extra click adds friction but not scrutiny, and more cases per hour removes even more time.

questions.question: A manager sets up an AI assistant to send routine replies to clients on her behalf. One reply promises a refund that she never approved. Who is accountable for that reply?
options: The manager, who configured the assistant and allowed it to act for her
Anthropic, because its model wrote the reply that contained the promise
The client, who should have checked the promise before relying on it
Nobody, because an AI's autonomous action cannot be attributed to a person
questions.explanation: People remain responsible for what they do with AI, and Anthropic's Usage Policy makes users responsible for agents they build or deploy. The manager chose the scope of the assistant's authority and should have kept an approval step for commitments such as refunds. Responsibility does not pass to the model, the vendor or the client.

questions.question: A housing agency uses Claude to review applications and propose a decision with reasons. A caseworker reviews each proposal, and the agency then sends the decision letter. Following the principle that people affected by high-risk decisions are told when AI was used, what should the letter do?
options: Omit any mention, since the caseworker's review makes the decision a human one
Say clearly that AI helped prepare the decision and that a caseworker reviewed it
Mention AI only if an applicant asks how the decision was reached
State the use of AI once in the agency's website footer instead of in the letters
questions.explanation: Housing and public benefits are high-risk areas in Anthropic's Usage Policy, which asks that a qualified person meaningfully review AI recommendations and that the affected individual be clearly told that AI was used. The caseworker's review satisfies the first duty but does not cancel the second, and disclosure on request or in a footer is not a clear notice to the person affected.

questions.question: Which TWO of these uses of Claude call for review by a qualified person before the output reaches the people affected? (Choose two.)
options: Summarizing the team's own meeting notes for an internal wiki
Recommending whether a customer's insurance claim should be paid
Brainstorming names for an internal project
Proposing which applicants should be approved for a rental home
Rewording the introduction of the team's own newsletter article
questions.explanation: Insurance and housing are high-risk areas: the output would feed a decision that significantly affects a person's money or home. Anthropic's Usage Policy asks for meaningful review by a qualified person with authority to change the result, and for the affected person to be told that AI was involved. The other three are assistive tasks in which a person uses the output for their own work.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to find themes in a customer-feedback export that has names, email addresses, phone numbers, account IDs, region and comment text. Which TWO steps best reduce privacy risk before uploading? (Choose two.)
options: Drop the columns the analysis does not need, such as email addresses, phone numbers and account IDs
Name the file 'anonymous_feedback' so that reviewers know it is safe
Tell Claude in the prompt to ignore any personal details it sees
Replace the remaining customer names with consistent codes and keep the lookup table out of the upload
Upload the export to a personal account whose model-improvement setting is switched off
questions.explanation: Minimize first by leaving out what the task does not need, then pseudonymize what remains so that rows stay distinguishable while the key stays elsewhere. A file name changes nothing about the content, an instruction to ignore details does not stop them being shared, and a personal account is outside the approved tools whatever its settings.

questions.question: A team wants to use Claude on personal data about customers in the European Union. Which TWO actions are most appropriate? (Choose two.)
options: Treat the vendor's security certifications as proof that the use is lawful
Ask the privacy or legal team whether there is a lawful basis and whether the account and terms in use are approved for personal data
Ask Claude whether the use complies with the law and follow its answer
Use an incognito chat so that the data is not stored
Send only the fields the task needs and leave out other personal details
questions.explanation: The GDPR requires a lawful basis, data minimization and respect for individuals' rights, and the privacy team decides whether the use meets them, including whether the vendor terms (such as a data processing addendum) are approved. Certifications support a vendor review but do not make your own use lawful, Claude can explain concepts but is not the compliance decision-maker, and incognito changes how Claude stores a chat, not whether the sharing was permitted.

questions.question: A company is rolling out Claude to its marketing team. Which TWO elements belong in a sound AI acceptable use policy? (Choose two.)
options: Which AI tools and accounts are approved, and which classes of data may be used with them
A statement that Claude's outputs are accurate enough that human review is optional
Who to contact with questions, and how to report a problem with AI output or data
A rule that staff should avoid telling clients when AI contributed to a deliverable
A ban on using Claude for any task that touches customer information
questions.explanation: A workable policy names the approved tools, the data allowed in each, the review and disclosure expectations, and an escalation route. Claiming that review is optional contradicts the need for verification, hiding AI use from clients runs against the transparency duties that many contracts and laws add, and a blanket ban on customer-related work is unnecessary when approved tools and data rules can manage the risk.

questions.question: A team shares a Claude Project that contains salary data for an HR review. Which TWO choices follow the principle of least privilege? (Choose two.)
options: Share the Project organization-wide so that anyone can find it when needed
Give everyone edit access so that mistakes can be fixed quickly
Share it only with the HR staff who need the data, with view-only access for those who do not edit
Enable every available connector in case one proves useful later
Leave out of the Project's knowledge any files the review does not need
questions.explanation: Least privilege gives each person and tool only the access the task needs: the smallest group, view-only where editing is not required, and no unneeded sensitive files in the knowledge. Organization-wide sharing, blanket edit rights and enabling every connector all widen access beyond what the work requires.

questions.question: A consultant is about to send a client a report that Claude helped draft. Which TWO actions reflect responsible, transparent use? (Choose two.)
options: Check the report's facts and figures against the sources, and take responsibility for what is sent
Remove any trace of AI involvement so that the client's trust in the report is not shaken
Ask Claude to certify that the report contains no errors, then send it
Send it as it is, because the draft was built from the firm's own documents
Follow the contract's and the firm's rules on telling clients when AI has contributed
questions.explanation: Diligence means verifying work before it is shared and being open about AI's role where contracts, policies or law call for it; the sender remains accountable. Concealing AI use, accepting Claude's own certification, or assuming that good sources guarantee a correct draft each skip part of that responsibility.

questions.question: Using Claude to draft an email that an executive reviews, edits and sends under her own name counts as the impersonation that Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits.
questions.explanation: Prohibited impersonation means posing as a real person or organization, or creating fake personas, in order to mislead others. Drafting help for someone who reviews the message and sends it as their own is ordinary assistance. The policy targets deception about who is really speaking.

questions.question: A consumer-facing chatbot built on Claude must tell users that they are interacting with an AI.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy requires AI disclosure to users, at least at the start of a chat session or in the product interface. The chatbot may have a friendly name and persona, but it must not pretend to be human.

questions.question: Claude can help you prepare questions and summarize documents for a meeting with a lawyer, but the lawyer, not Claude, gives the advice you rely on.
questions.explanation: This is the professional-advice boundary. Claude's answers on legal, medical, tax or investment questions are information to take to a qualified professional, who gives the advice and carries the responsibility. Using Claude to prepare for that conversation is a sensible, low-risk use.

questions.question: Replacing employee names with codes while keeping a separate table that links each code to a person makes the data anonymous.
questions.explanation: This is pseudonymization. Because the linking key still exists, people can be re-identified, so the data can still count as personal data and needs protection. Anonymization has to prevent identification even when the data is combined with other information.

questions.question: Because incognito chats are not saved to history or memory, a company's rules about which data may be shared with AI tools do not apply to them.
questions.explanation: Incognito changes how Claude stores and uses the conversation, not what an employer allows its staff to share. The rule about what may be pasted into an AI tool applies in every kind of chat, and on Team and Enterprise plans incognito chats still follow organizational retention.

questions.question: A vendor's SOC 2 report and ISO certifications can support a vendor risk review, but they do not by themselves settle whether your own use of the tool is lawful and allowed.
questions.explanation: Certifications and audit reports are evidence about the vendor's controls and governance processes. Whether your own use is lawful and permitted depends on your data, your contracts, your regulators and your policy, which the privacy, legal and security teams assess.

questions.question: On Anthropic's individual plans, whether conversations may be used to improve models depends on a privacy setting that the account holder controls.
questions.explanation: The individual plans (Free, Pro and Max) have a model-improvement setting, and incognito chats are excluded even when it is on. Anthropic's commercial products (Team, Enterprise and the API) do not use inputs and outputs for training by default. Knowing which terms apply to the account you are using is part of handling sensitive data.

questions.question: If a company's AI policy says nothing about a particular situation, employees can assume the situation is permitted.
questions.explanation: Silence is not permission. When the policy does not cover a situation, the right step is to ask the policy owner, such as IT, security or compliance, and to stay within approved tools and data rules until they answer.

questions.question: When a person connects her own Google Drive to Claude, Claude can read only the files that she is already permitted to open.
questions.explanation: Connectors work through the signed-in person's own permissions and never grant more access than the source system allows; administrators can narrow what is available but not widen it. This is why access reviews and least privilege on the source system matter.

questions.question: If a piece of text carries no AI watermark, that shows it was written by a person.
questions.explanation: Marks are added only to output from supported models and can be lost through editing or conversion. A detected mark is a signal, not proof, and a missing mark proves nothing, so the absence of a mark never means that a person wrote the text.

questions.question: A team keeps a troubleshooting sheet that pairs a common symptom of weak Claude output with a first fix to try. Which pairing on the sheet is correct?
options: Plausible figures that match nothing in the attached files: ask for a more formal tone
A different layout on every run: describe the layout and show a sample to copy
A reply that stops partway through: shrink the files attached to the chat
A rule near the end of a long prompt that is skipped: repeat it in capital letters five times
questions.explanation: Match the fix to the cause. A layout that changes between runs comes from leaving the format open, so describe it and show a sample. Figures that match no file point to missing or unused source material, so tone is irrelevant; the fix is to supply the material and let Claude say when something is not in it. A reply cut off partway is continued by giving Claude the original request and the part already written and asking for the rest in sections. A skipped rule is fixed by making it prominent, positive and free of conflicts, not by shouting.

questions.question: A trainer asks Claude for 'a detailed outline for a safety workshop' and gets five terse bullets. She wants something she can teach from. What is the most effective fix?
options: Resend the same request several times and keep whichever reply happens to be the longest
Add 'try harder' and 'make it much longer' to the end of the request and send it again
Split the outline into five separate requests, each asking for a single bullet on one topic
Define 'detailed': the sections wanted, the amount for each, the audience, and a sample of the depth
questions.explanation: Replies come back thin when the request leaves depth to Claude's judgment. Naming the sections, the amount for each, the audience and an example of the depth wanted gives Claude a target. Resending the same request only resamples the same gap, vague pressure such as 'try harder' adds no information, and splitting the outline into fragments loses its overall structure.

questions.question: A team's Project instructions say 'Keep every answer to two sentences' near the top and 'Always explain your reasoning in full detail' lower down. Staff complain that answers are sometimes terse and sometimes long. What is the best fix?
options: Rewrite the instructions with a priority, such as brief by default and detailed only when asked
Add 'follow all instructions exactly' at the top of the Project instructions and keep both rules
Delete the Project's knowledge files in case the documents are what is causing the variation
Ask staff to keep regenerating any answer whose length they dislike until one of them fits
questions.explanation: The two rules cannot both be satisfied, so Claude has to choose, and the choice varies from conversation to conversation. Resolving the conflict with an explicit priority removes the variation at its cause. A general demand to follow everything cannot satisfy rules that contradict each other, the knowledge files are not the source of the inconsistency, and regenerating pushes the burden onto every user.

questions.question: Forty messages into a long analysis chat, Claude stops using the table layout and citation style that the analyst set up at the beginning. What is the best way to get back on track?
options: Keep going in the same chat and repeat 'follow the format' each time it slips, as often as needed
Ask Claude to rate how well it remembers the original instructions, and continue if the rating is high
Start a new chat with a short summary and the key rules, and move standing rules into Project instructions
Switch to the smallest available model, since smaller models follow formatting rules more closely
questions.explanation: In long conversations early instructions are gradually crowded out by newer material, which is called instruction drift. A fresh chat that begins with a concise, checked summary and the key rules restores focus, and placing standing rules in Project instructions makes them apply from the first message of every chat. Nagging treats each slip separately, a self-rating is not a fix, and a smaller model does nothing about rules fading from a long conversation.

questions.question: Two analysts give Claude the same request to label support tickets 'urgent' or 'routine' and get noticeably different splits. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?
options: Claude is malfunctioning; report the difference as a product bug and wait for the fix before using it
The model is too small; move to the largest model available and keep the request exactly the same
The labels are undefined; define each one with criteria, add borderline examples and fix the output layout
Each analyst should run the request three times and keep the label that appears most often per ticket
questions.explanation: Variation usually comes from open questions that Claude has to interpret: what counts as urgent, how to treat borderline tickets, what the answer should look like. Defining the labels, showing examples of tricky tickets and fixing the layout make results repeatable. It is not a malfunction, a larger model still has to guess at undefined labels, and voting across runs hides the underlying ambiguity instead of removing it.

questions.question: A finance analyst asks Claude for her company's third-quarter headcount by region and receives a confident table that does not match HR's records. Rewording the question produces different numbers each time. What is the real problem, and what is the best fix?
options: Claude lacks the company's data; supply the HR export, or connect the source, and have it answer only from that
The prompt lacks emphasis; add 'be accurate' and 'double-check every number' as the first lines of the request
Reasoning depth is too low; switch on extended thinking and ask the same question again so that it works harder
The question is too short; ask it in five different ways and use the numbers that come up most often
questions.explanation: Headcount is private company data that Claude cannot know, so any numbers it produces are invented, which is why they change with each rewording. This is a knowledge gap that wording cannot fix; the remedy is to supply the material (attach it, connect it or search) and restrict the answer to it, allowing 'not in the data' as an answer. Extra emphasis, deeper reasoning and repeated asking do not add facts.

questions.question: An associate pastes a very long report into a chat and sees 'Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat.' What is the best next step?
options: Send the same message again after a few minutes, in case the limit was only a temporary glitch
Tell Claude to keep its answers short, so that more of the report fits into the conversation
Sign out, sign back in and paste the report again, which resets the length limit for the chat
Split the report into sections or select the relevant parts, then combine the results afterwards
questions.explanation: The notice means the input is too large for the conversation, so the fix is to reduce or divide it: split the document, summarize or select the relevant sections, or start a new chat with the parts that matter, keeping a running list so that nothing is lost between parts. Retrying the same message changes nothing, the limit concerns what is sent rather than the length of Claude's reply, and signing in again has no effect on message size.

questions.question: Claude declines two requests. A teacher asked for a one-page overview of a historical atrocity for a lesson, and the reply seems to have misread her purpose. A marketing manager asked for fake customer testimonials. How should each be handled?
options: Rewrite both requests in different words, again and again, until Claude agrees to produce the content
Add the teacher's purpose and audience and ask again; accept the limit on testimonials and gather real ones instead
Accept both refusals without comment and drop both tasks, since a refusal means the task is unsuitable
Switch to another model for both requests, since a different model may be more willing to comply
questions.explanation: When a request was probably misread, stating the legitimate purpose and audience can resolve it. When a request conflicts with usage policy, as fake testimonials do, it is a boundary to respect and not a puzzle to solve by rewording or switching tools; the useful move is to ask for a legitimate alternative. Treating both the same way would either disguise a prohibited use or abandon a legitimate one.

questions.question: A team improved a contract-summary prompt by changing six things at once: role, format, length, tone, examples and order. Results got better, but nobody knows which change helped, and the next contract type broke it. What should the team do next time?
options: Make even more changes at once next time, so that the team moves faster toward a perfect prompt
Undo all six changes, return to the original prompt and stop work on this prompt for good
Ask Claude which of the six changes made the difference and take its answer as the explanation
Change one element at a time and rerun the same test contracts, to see each change's effect
questions.explanation: Changing one thing at a time against the same test inputs isolates cause and effect, so the team keeps what helps and drops what does not. Bundling changes hides which one worked, more bundled changes make it worse, giving up discards a real improvement, and Claude cannot reliably say which edit mattered; comparing runs is what shows it.

questions.question: A team has rewritten a prompt ten times to reconcile invoice totals across three systems that store data in different formats, but the last six edits barely changed the results. The job needs exact matching across thousands of rows. What is the best next step?
options: Keep refining the wording, since a sufficiently clear prompt will eventually produce exact matches
Stop rewording and hand the matching to a technical colleague, keeping Claude for the rules and samples
Switch to a larger model and resend the latest version of the prompt unchanged, to see if it copes
Ask each analyst to write a personal version of the prompt and use the one with the highest total
questions.explanation: Several edits with little gain are a sign of diminishing returns: the obstacle is not the wording. Exact matching at scale is technical work for a developer or analyst with proper tooling, while Claude can still help define the rules and review samples. More polishing, a bigger model or competing prompts repeat the same approach.

questions.question: After a month, a team finds that Claude-drafted answers to billing questions are used unedited about 90% of the time, but answers to technical product questions only about 30% of the time. How should the team adjust its approach?
options: Apply the billing prompt to every question type, since it clearly works well and is already in use
Stop using Claude for the help desk altogether, since the technical answers fall short of the goal
Keep using Claude for billing; for technical questions add product documents and route drafts to a specialist
Add 'be accurate and thorough' to the technical prompt and measure the results again next quarter
questions.explanation: Results should shape the approach: keep what works and adapt what does not. The technical gap is probably missing source material and a need for expert review, so supplying documentation and routing drafts to a specialist addresses the cause. Treating all question types alike ignores the data, abandoning the tool discards a proven use, and an exhortation to be accurate adds no information.

questions.question: A communications team wants to know whether a new version of its press-summary prompt really beats the current one. Which method gives the most trustworthy answer?
options: Run both versions on the same set of past releases and score the results against the same criteria
Run the new version on this week's easy release and the current version on last year's complicated one
Ask Claude which of the two prompts is better and adopt its choice
Adopt whichever version the most senior person prefers after reading one output of each
questions.explanation: A fair comparison holds the inputs and the scoring criteria constant, so any difference comes from the prompt. Different inputs confound the result, Claude's opinion about prompts is not evidence of how they perform on your documents, and one output judged by seniority is an anecdote.

questions.question: An analyst sends Claude twelve short, related questions about the same survey one at a time and reaches her usage limit by mid-afternoon. Which change most reduces usage without lowering the quality of the answers?
options: Group the related questions into one organized message, with the survey attached once
Ask for shorter answers and keep sending the twelve questions one by one as they occur
Open a new chat for each question and re-attach the survey file each time it is needed
Switch to the most capable model for every question, so that fewer follow-ups are needed
questions.explanation: Anthropic's usage guidance recommends batching related requests into one message and not repeating material. Grouping gives Claude the full picture and avoids re-sending context. Fresh chats that re-attach the survey repeat the cost, shorter answers trim only part of it, and model choice is one of the factors that use the allowance faster, so the most capable model is not the economical default.

questions.question: After a long chat, a product manager finally gets Claude to write release notes in exactly the right voice. Two weeks later she cannot reproduce the result in a new chat. What should she have done?
options: Kept that chat open indefinitely and written every new set of release notes inside that chat
Asked Claude to remember that the voice was right and to apply it to every future set of notes
Saved the winning prompt, with a sample of good output, as a reusable template or Project instruction
Taken a screenshot of the final output and pasted the image into each new chat as a model to copy
questions.explanation: A prompt that finally works is easily lost in a long chat. Capturing it at once, with an example of good output, makes the success repeatable and shareable, and a Project instruction or skill carries it into new chats. A chat kept open grows unwieldy and drifts, memory holds short notes about you rather than a dependable recipe, and a screenshot shows one result but not the instructions that produced it.

questions.question: A team's Claude-drafted client emails now take 40% less time to produce, but reviewers rewrite about half of them before sending. What does this suggest?
options: The workflow is a clear success, because first drafts now arrive much faster than they did before
The real gain may be small; the team should find why drafts need so much rework and improve the prompt
The team should add more reviewers so that the rewriting is shared and each person has less to do
The team should remove the review step to save time, since reviewers are rewriting the drafts anyway
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the time to a usable result, not the time to a first draft. A high rework rate eats the saving, so the team should diagnose the cause, such as missing context, an unclear style or conflicting instructions, and fix it. Declaring success measures the wrong thing, more reviewers spread the cost instead of lowering it, and removing review would let the flawed drafts go out.

questions.question: A team's Claude-assisted proposals are drafted in five minutes, yet each one still takes three days to reach the client because it waits in a queue for a single manager's approval. Where should the team focus its optimization effort?
options: On making the draft even faster than five minutes, since drafting is the step Claude supports
On removing the approval step entirely, so that proposals are sent out as soon as they are drafted
On trying other models to see whether one produces drafts that get the manager to approve sooner
On the approval step, for example with clear criteria, a backup approver or pre-checked drafts
questions.explanation: A process moves only as fast as its bottleneck, which here is the approval queue; speeding up drafting further changes almost nothing about the total time. Clear criteria, a backup approver or pre-checked drafts shorten the wait while keeping the checkpoint. Dropping approval altogether sacrifices control, and the choice of model has no influence on the manager's availability.

questions.question: Analysts run the same prompt every day and get correct content, but the layout changes from run to run. Which TWO changes are most likely to make the results consistent? (Choose two.)
options: Describe the layout explicitly, with named sections or columns
Add a sentence asking Claude to be consistent
Include one or two examples of the exact output wanted
Run it three times and use the middle result
Ask for a more creative answer
questions.explanation: Consistency comes from structure: a defined layout and examples to copy remove the open choices that Claude would otherwise make differently each time. 'Be consistent' states a wish without saying what to be consistent with, picking a middle result accepts the variation instead of removing it, and asking for creativity pulls the other way.

questions.question: Claude can no longer open a Google Drive file that it read last week, and prompts the user to reconnect. Which TWO are sensible first steps? (Choose two.)
options: Rewrite the prompt with more background about the file
Disconnect and sign in again to the Drive connector in the connector settings
Move the file into a different Project
Check whether the person's own access to the file has changed, or whether an administrator has to approve the app
Tell Claude to ignore the access error and answer without the file
questions.explanation: A reconnect prompt points to an access or authentication problem, not a wording problem. Signing in again often clears it, and because a connector sees only what the signed-in person can open, her own permissions or an administrator's approval may be the cause. Rewriting the prompt treats a problem that is not there, moving the file does not repair authentication, and answering without the file invites invented content.

questions.question: A team has been tweaking a prompt for a report on competitors' pricing. Which TWO signs show that it is time to change approach rather than keep rewording? (Choose two.)
options: The initial reply was good except for one awkward sentence
The output is slightly longer than the team prefers
Several rounds of edits have produced almost no improvement
A reviewer asked for a different heading style
The report needs current competitor prices that Claude has never been given
questions.explanation: Little gain after repeated edits is diminishing returns, and missing facts are a knowledge gap that wording cannot close; both call for a different approach, such as supplying sources, using web search or involving a person who has the data. An awkward sentence, a slightly long output and a heading preference are small, targeted fixes within the same approach.

questions.question: A team wants to reduce rework on a weekly report that Claude drafts. Which TWO actions are most likely to help? (Choose two.)
options: Ask reviewers to accept the first draft unless it is far off
Keep the report template and a sample of an approved report in a Project, so that every draft starts from them
Switch to a different prompt each week to keep the results fresh
Remove the review step once the drafts look good
Track the corrections reviewers make, and update the instructions to prevent the most common ones
questions.explanation: Rework falls when drafts start from the right template and examples and when recurring corrections feed back into the instructions. Lowering the bar for review pushes errors downstream, changing the prompt every week prevents the team from learning what works, and dropping review is over-automation.

questions.question: When Claude lacks facts it needs, such as private company figures, rewording the request will not help; the material has to be supplied.
questions.explanation: A knowledge gap is not a wording problem. Attach the document, connect the source or use search, and ask Claude to answer only from that material and to say when something is not in it. Without the material, Claude can only produce plausible-sounding guesses.

questions.question: If Claude declines a request because it conflicts with Anthropic's usage policies, rephrasing the request to hide its purpose is an acceptable troubleshooting step.
questions.explanation: A policy boundary is a limit to respect, not a puzzle to get around. If the request was simply misread, restate the legitimate purpose and audience plainly; if it really conflicts with policy, look for a legitimate alternative or take the need to someone who can authorize it.

questions.question: A message saying that Claude is temporarily limited by capacity constraints means the prompt is too long, so the fix is to shorten the request.
questions.explanation: A capacity message reflects heavy demand on the service, not a defect in the request, so rewriting the prompt does not help; wait a few minutes and retry, and check Anthropic's status page if errors persist. A request that is too long produces a different notice, that the message will exceed the length limit for the chat.

questions.question: A prompt that gave good results on a handful of tidy sample documents can be assumed to work on every kind of real document.
questions.explanation: Tidy samples hide failures. Testing with unusual inputs, such as empty fields, odd formats, very long text and conflicting data, finds where a prompt or workflow breaks before real use.

questions.question: Keeping dated copies of each prompt version, with a note of what changed, lets a team restore a version that worked if a later 'improvement' makes results worse.
questions.explanation: Without versions, a change that made things worse cannot be undone with confidence. A short note on what changed and how results moved also shows which edits are worth keeping.

questions.question: Documents kept in a Project count less against usage limits when they are reused, although that benefit lapses after a period of inactivity.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's usage guidance says that cached content counts less when it is reused and that the cache expires after inactivity. That is a reason to keep recurring documents in a Project and to ask related questions together.

lessons.title: Writing Prompts That Get Useful Results
lessons.summary: What to put in a request so Claude can do good work: background, a direct task, format, constraints, examples, clear structure and a reusable template.
lessons.reading:
Claude starts every conversation knowing nothing about your company, your reader or why you are asking. Anthropic compares it to a brilliant new colleague who lacks context on your norms: very capable, but only as good as the briefing. Everything Claude can use has to be in the conversation, typed or attached. That is why 'Write a job posting' produces something generic, while 'Write a posting for a project coordinator on a six-person operations team, aimed at career changers, friendly but precise, under 300 words, with separate responsibilities and requirements' produces something you can use. A quick check is the colleague test: if a coworker with no background would be confused by your request, Claude probably will be too.

Four ingredients do most of the work. First, background: the purpose, the reader and the situation. Second, the task, stated directly, including any extra effort you want, since Claude will not assume it. Third, the output format: a table with named columns, five bullets, a 150-word email. Fourth, constraints such as length, reading level, tone or the sources to rely on. Phrase them as what to do rather than what to avoid: 'write three short paragraphs in plain language for busy readers' steers better than 'don't be wordy'. When a rule is not obvious, say why. 'Avoid idioms, because this text will be machine-translated' lets Claude apply the intent to idioms you never listed, whereas a bare ban is followed narrowly. The same habits apply to technical tasks such as a spreadsheet formula or an error message: paste the exact error, say which application you use, and state the result you expect.

Examples are among the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Instead of describing the weekly summary you want, paste two good ones and ask for this week's in the same shape. One example is a fine start; Anthropic recommends three to five when you need consistency. They should be relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases (urgency tags taught only from cheerful tickets will mishandle angry ones), and clearly labeled as examples.

Structure matters once a request mixes kinds of content. Separate your instructions from pasted material with plain labels such as 'Notes:', 'Template:' and 'Instructions:', so Claude never mistakes a sentence in the notes for something you asked it to do. With a long document, put the document first and your question after it; Anthropic's tests found that placing the query at the end improves results, especially with several documents. When you attach files, say which file and which part you mean, and remember how files are read: for PDFs up to 100 pages Claude looks at text and visuals such as charts, longer PDFs are processed as text only, and for Word and similar files only the text is extracted.

A role helps when it names a perspective and what that perspective cares about: 'review this as a skeptical procurement lead who cares most about renewal terms and hidden fees' beats 'you are the world's best negotiator'. Roles are optional and never replace real information. When a prompt works, keep it. A shared template with fixed instructions and placeholders such as [report] and [audience] keeps recurring work consistent across people and months.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to prompting? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine briefing a temp worker on their first day. If you say 'make the quarterly deck', you will get something generic. If you say who the audience is, what the deck is meant to achieve, which template to use, what last quarter's deck looked like and when it is due, they can do good work in an hour. Claude is the quick, well-read, eager temp who has never seen your company. The prompt is the briefing.
commonTraps: A short, vague request is not efficient: missing audience, purpose and format are the main reasons for generic output.
Telling Claude only what to avoid ("don't be wordy") is weaker than describing the result you want.
More examples are not better if they are all alike; examples must be relevant and varied.
Pasting everything into one unlabeled block invites Claude to treat source text as instructions; separate and label the parts.
PDFs longer than 100 pages are read as text only, and non-PDF files lose their embedded images, so a chart you care about may never be seen.
lessons.scenario: A communications specialist is asked for an announcement about a new expense policy. Her first prompt, 'Write an announcement about the new expense policy', returns a stiff, generic memo. She rewrites it: the readers are 400 field staff, the goal is receipts submitted within five days, the tone should match two earlier announcements pasted in as examples, the length is 200 words, and the policy document is attached with an instruction to quote the deadline exactly. The second draft needs only a small edit.
lessons.onTheJob: Build a personal library of prompts that worked. When one gets a good result, save it with placeholders for the parts that change and a note about what it was for. Before sending a request that matters, reread it as a stranger would: audience, purpose, format, limits, source. If you catch yourself writing 'you know what I mean', you are relying on context Claude cannot see. Paste only the material the task needs, and follow your organization's rules about what may be shared.

lessons.title: Breaking Down Tasks, Iterating and Matching the Task Type
lessons.summary: How to split big jobs into checkable stages, improve results through targeted feedback, and adapt your request for analysis, research, drafting and brainstorming.
lessons.reading:
A large request fails in a predictable way. Ask Claude in one message to read 200 survey comments, group them into themes, rank the themes by revenue impact, propose actions and draft a board email, and each stage gets a quick pass, while a mistake in the first stage flows silently into the last. Task decomposition is the fix: split the job into stages with one purpose each, in a sensible order, so every stage gets full attention and can be checked. 'Each prompt should do one thing well' is a good rule of thumb.

Prompt chaining runs the stages as a sequence in which each answer becomes the input to the next: extract the themes, then rank them, then recommend actions, then draft the email. The cost is speed; the benefit is accuracy and control, because you can read an intermediate result and fix it before it spreads. A common pattern is the self-correction chain: produce a draft, ask Claude to review it against criteria you state (audience fit, risks covered, numbers sourced), then ask for a revision. When one request holds several steps whose order matters, number them: '1. extract dates, 2. flag conflicts, 3. draft the recap'. For a problem that is hard rather than long, such as a scheduling puzzle with many constraints, asking Claude to work step by step, or using extended thinking, is the right tool, and the result still needs checking. Do not over-engineer: a short, single-purpose task needs no chain.

Treat the first answer as a draft. Before you start, write down success criteria: who will read it, what it must cover, how long it should be, what accuracy bar applies. Judge the output against them and give targeted feedback. 'Keep the refund details, cut to about 100 words, friendlier tone' converges quickly; 'try again' and 'make it better' make Claude guess. Change one thing at a time so you can tell what helped. Start with a plain, short prompt and add structure only when a specific shortfall calls for it. Prompts that gain a new rule after every disappointment end up long and self-contradictory, and the cure is to cut back to a core request and re-add only what earns its place. If a request is genuinely ambiguous, invite Claude to ask you questions before it starts.

Different tasks need different emphasis. For analysis, supply the data, state the question and the decision it feeds, name the metrics, and ask Claude to show its method and assumptions so you can check them. For research, say what a complete answer must cover, ask Claude to cross-check across several sources, flag conflicts and gaps, and give links; when you need current web information, use web search or the research mode instead of relying on memory. For drafting, name the reader, purpose, tone and length, show samples of the voice you want, and refine in rounds. For brainstorming, ask for many options that differ in angle, tone or approach, and narrow them with criteria afterward; asking for 'the best idea' first collapses the variety.

Whatever the task, the loop is the same: brief, run, check against your criteria, give specific feedback, and save what worked. Chains and templates turn a good result into a repeatable one, which is what makes Claude useful for recurring business work rather than a one-off trick.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to task decomposition? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of cooking a banquet. You would not throw every ingredient into one pot and hope. You prep, cook each dish separately, taste as you go and adjust the seasoning one pinch at a time. Decomposing a task is the prep and the separate dishes, iteration is the tasting and adjusting, and matching the task type is choosing the right cooking method for each dish.
commonTraps: Chaining is not always better: it trades speed for control, so use it when you need checkpoints or each stage needs different input, not for a simple one-step task.
Adding more and louder rules to a long prompt usually makes it worse; cut back and re-add only what solves an observed problem.
"Try again" and "make it better" are not feedback; name what to keep and what to change.
Brainstorming asks for many varied options first and judges later, analysis shows assumptions, and research needs sources and cross-checking.
Extended thinking helps with hard reasoning, but it does not replace checking the answer and it does not fetch fresh information.
lessons.scenario: A project manager has 200 free-text survey comments and a board meeting on Friday. She asks Claude to group the comments into themes with five example quotes each, reads the grouping, merges two themes and renames one. Next she asks for the themes ranked by how many comments mention cost and the counts shown. Then she asks for three recommended actions with the evidence for each, and finally for a one-page board email in the style of a previous email she pastes in. At each stage she corrects before moving on, and the final email survives a read-through without surprises.
lessons.onTheJob: Decide the stages before you start and write down the check that tells you each one is done. Keep intermediate results in the conversation so later steps can use them, and keep a short list of the corrections you make most often; those become rules in your template. When a chat gets long and tangled, summarize the decisions and restart with a clean prompt. Share a chain with your team as a checklist of prompts, not as one giant instruction nobody can debug.

lessons.title: Spotting Hallucinations and Validating What Claude Tells You
lessons.summary: The ways Claude output goes wrong, what does and does not count as verification, and prompting techniques that make errors rarer and easier to catch.
lessons.reading:
Claude writes fluent, confident text whether or not the content is right. A hallucination is a statement that is false or unsupported but reads as plausible: an invented statistic, a quotation nobody said, a case that does not exist, a section number that points nowhere. Anthropic is direct: the techniques that reduce hallucinations do not eliminate them, and critical information must still be validated, especially for high-stakes decisions. The Help Center adds that Claude should not be your only source of truth. Read Claude's output as a capable colleague's first draft: fast, useful and in need of checking.

Learn the common failure shapes. Fabricated details: specific-looking figures, quotes and citations. Stale knowledge: training data stops at a cutoff, so new rules, prices and releases are unknown unless web search or an attached document supplies them. Internal inconsistency: the summary says 18% and section three says 15%. Omissions: five action items from a transcript that holds nine. Claimed actions: Claude says it emailed the summary or produced a link, when without a connected tool it did neither, so confirm outside actions where they should exist and click every link. Arithmetic slips: recheck important calculations in a spreadsheet. Keep two questions apart. Accuracy asks whether what is said is right; completeness asks whether everything required is present. An output can pass one and fail the other.

Be clear about what is not verification. A confident tone is not evidence. Asking Claude 'are you sure?' or 'rate your confidence' is not evidence either, because the answer comes from the same source as the original claim. Running the request again and getting the same answer shows consistency, not truth. Real verification comes from outside: the primary source (the report, contract or official text), an independent recalculation, a second reliable source, or a person with expertise. Web-search answers come with citations, which make checking possible, but the check is yours: open the sources, confirm they say what is claimed, and judge whether they are current and credible. The Help Center advises reviewing cited sources, since original pages may hold context a summary omits.

You can also write prompts that make errors rarer and easier to catch. Give Claude permission to say it does not know, or that the document does not say. For long documents, ask for word-for-word quotes first and base the analysis on them, so every claim can be located, and tell Claude to use only the material you supplied. After a draft, ask for a supporting passage for each claim and for unsupported claims to be removed, then spot-check the passages yourself. Running a request several times can expose unstable claims, and the thinking summary, or a request to lay out the steps, often reveals a faulty assumption. For big outputs such as 500 classified tickets, check a random sample plus the ambiguous cases before trusting the rest.

Scale the effort to the stakes. A brainstorm needs a quick read; a figure headed for a regulator needs tracing to its source. Check specifics first (numbers, names, dates, citations, quoted text), because that is where fabrication hides, then compare the work with a requirements checklist written before you read it.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to checking AI output? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture an intern who is brilliant at drafting but never says 'I'm not sure' and now and then fills a gap with something that merely sounds right. You would not forward their memo to the regulator unchecked. You would read it, ask where a number came from and look at the original document. Verifying Claude works the same way: the more the memo matters, the more carefully you check the sources.
commonTraps: Asking Claude to confirm its own answer, or to rate its confidence, is not verification.
Citations in a search answer make checking possible; they do not make the claim true, so open them.
Extended thinking improves reasoning but does not give Claude newer facts; recent changes need web search or a supplied source.
A response can be accurate and still incomplete; check both against the request.
If Claude says it sent an email or created a file outside the chat, confirm it where it should exist.
lessons.scenario: A marketing analyst asks Claude for three statistics on short-video growth for a board slide, and Claude supplies figures with named sources. She asks for the passage behind each figure and tries to find each one in the cited report. One figure belongs to a different year, and one report does not appear to exist. She replaces the first with the correct number, drops the second, and lists the verified sources in the speaker notes.
lessons.onTheJob: Build verification into the workflow instead of relying on mood. Ask for sources at the time of the request so checking is cheaper later, keep a short checklist per document type (contracts: dates, amounts, clause numbers; reports: figures, names, units), and note which items you verified. Treat anything surprising, very specific or time-sensitive as a flag. And remember that you, not Claude, are accountable for what leaves your desk.

lessons.title: Bias, Human Review, Editing for Audiences and Choosing Output Formats
lessons.summary: How to test for bias, decide when a person must review, adapt and compare drafts, curate information, and pick between inline answers, artifacts, structured data and created files.
lessons.reading:
Bias in AI output is a systematic tilt: stereotypes, one-sided framing, uneven treatment of people or viewpoints, or perspectives left out. It can come from training-data patterns, from how a question is asked, and from a tendency to agree with the asker, called sycophancy. A request like 'Explain why remote work hurts productivity' presupposes its answer and returns a persuasive essay; 'Summarize the evidence on remote work and productivity, including findings in both directions, with sources' returns something you can evaluate. Ask 'This plan is solid, right?' and expect agreement; ask instead for the strongest objections, or for a review as a skeptical investor.

Run the same request again with one personal detail changed, such as a name, a gender or a region, and compare the language and conclusions; this swap test suits performance reviews and screening criteria. Ask for multiple perspectives and the main counterarguments. Look at what is missing, not only at what is said. In areas such as hiring, lending, health and education, have people who understand the domain review the output. Claude's own statement that it is unbiased is not evidence.

Deciding when a human must review is a judgment about consequences. High-stakes output is content whose errors could cause legal, financial, medical, safety, regulatory or reputational harm, or affect an individual's job or access to services: contract clauses, patient guidance, filings, decisions about a named employee. For those, qualified review by counsel, an accountant or a clinician is part of the workflow. Lower-stakes drafts such as internal agendas and brainstorms need a lighter check. Beware automation bias, the habit of trusting output because it looks polished. Whoever sends or publishes the content remains responsible for it.

Much of the work is editing and adapting. To tailor a report for executives and engineers, name each reader, what they need and the length ('executives, decision needed, 150 words'), then check the rewrite against the original, because shortening can turn 'may' into 'will' or drop a condition. To change one passage, highlight it and ask Claude to revise only that part. To choose between options, ask for two or three variants that differ in a stated way and compare them against criteria, or edit an earlier message to branch the conversation and keep both paths. To curate, give criteria for what to keep and how to group, and ask for a synthesis rather than a pile of summaries: a table of claims by source with conflicts flagged.

Choose the output format for the use. Short, conversational answers stay inline. Substantial, self-contained content you will edit, reuse or share, such as a policy template or a small interactive tool, suits an artifact, which opens beside the chat, is saved, and stays private until you share it. Data that will be sorted, filtered or imported should be structured: a table or CSV with fixed columns, one row per record and a rule for missing values. When you need a real file, Claude can build Excel workbooks with working formulas, Word documents, PowerPoint decks and PDFs when code execution and file creation is switched on. Whatever the format, review before it goes anywhere: generated formulas, numbers and wording can be wrong.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to reviewing AI drafts? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A newspaper editor does several jobs on one draft. They check that the story is fair to every side, decide whether a lawyer must see it before it runs, rewrite the headline for a different audience, and choose whether it belongs in print, online or as a chart. Reviewing Claude's output is the same set of editorial decisions.
commonTraps: Asking Claude whether it is biased is not a bias check; a swap test or expert review is.
Warm agreement from Claude is not validation of your plan; ask for the strongest objections.
A rewrite for a new audience can change meaning, so recheck it against the original.
Artifacts are for substantial, self-contained, editable content, while short answers belong inline.
Generated files and formulas still need review; being produced by code does not make them right.
lessons.scenario: An HR coordinator asks Claude to draft screening criteria for a customer-service hiring round, and the draft includes 'digital native' and 'high energy'. She asks for job-related criteria instead, runs the rubric request twice with different candidate names to compare the results, and asks for the strongest arguments against the rubric. Because it will affect real candidates, she sends the final version to HR for review, then asks Claude to put the approved rubric in an artifact she can edit and share with interviewers.
lessons.onTheJob: Write down which kinds of output in your team always need a named human reviewer, and put that in your template so nobody decides under deadline pressure. Keep the original beside every adapted version and spot-check numbers and qualifiers. When you compare variants, say what you are optimizing for. And ask for the format you need at the start: converting a prose answer into a clean table afterward is possible but invites transcription errors.

lessons.title: Choosing Features, Models and Managing Context
lessons.summary: Which Claude feature fits which job, how the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus tiers and the effort setting trade quality, speed and cost, and how to manage context and memory.
lessons.reading:
Pick the feature before the model. Standard chat is the default for quick questions, drafting and iteration. Web search pulls current information with citations for lookups that take a search or two. Extended thinking lets Claude reason through a hard problem but does not fetch new information. Research is for big questions: many searches that build on each other across the web and your enabled integrations, ending in a cited report. It takes minutes, needs web search on, is limited to paid plans and uses your allowance faster. A Project keeps shared files, instructions and chats together, so use one when you keep re-pasting the same brief. An artifact holds substantial, editable output, including small interactive tools. Use the lightest option that fits, and confirm that your plan allows it.

The tiers trade capability against speed and cost. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest, suited to high-volume work such as classification, extraction and routing. Sonnet is the balanced middle tier, Anthropic's best mix of speed and intelligence, and a sensible default for everyday drafting and analysis. Opus is the high-capability tier for demanding, nuanced work, at moderate speed and a higher price. The current lineup also has Fable above Opus, the most capable, slowest and costliest. Efficiency-first selection starts small, tests against your criteria and moves up only where quality falls short; capability-first starts with the strongest option where accuracy outweighs cost. The top tier for everything wastes time and allowance; the smallest for subtle judgment wastes the result.

The model menu beside the send button also holds effort and thinking, and you can change any of the three mid-conversation; the change applies from the next response. Higher effort, from low to max, is more thorough but slower and reaches your usage limits faster, so low and medium suit routine work. Anthropic notes that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. A workflow can draft on a lighter model, then switch to a stronger one for the polish.

Context is the other constraint. The context window is everything Claude can consider at once, your messages, its replies, attachments and instructions, counted in tokens; it is working memory. A bigger window is not used equally well throughout: accuracy and recall degrade as material piles up, which Anthropic calls context rot, so curate what you include. On paid plans with code execution enabled, Claude summarizes earlier messages automatically near the limit, but long chats use more of your allowance. Restart when a thread has drifted, gathered contradictory instructions or grown so long that early details slip: ask for a handoff summary of decisions and open questions, correct it, and paste it into a new chat. Material you reuse belongs in a Project.

Memory carries details about you across chats. Chat memory saves useful details as editable topics under Settings > Memory and uses them in later chats; each Project keeps its own memory. For a one-off or unrelated task, switch memory off from the plus menu before the first message, since it cannot be changed once the chat starts. If memory holds something outdated, edit or delete that topic rather than resetting everything.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Claude models? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a model is like choosing a vehicle. A bicycle (Haiku) is perfect for quick errands, a sedan (Sonnet) handles most daily driving, and a heavy truck (Opus) is for the big load, but you would not take the truck to buy milk or the bicycle to move an apartment. The features are route options: a quick lookup (web search), a full survey trip (research), or thinking about the route before leaving (extended thinking). Context is the trunk: it holds a lot, but an overloaded trunk makes the ride worse.
commonTraps: Extended thinking improves reasoning; it does not add current information. For recent facts use web search or research.
Research is not a faster web search; it is slower, deeper and uses allowance faster, so keep it for multi-source investigations.
The most capable model is not always the best choice; match the model and effort to the task.
A larger context window does not mean everything in it is used well; curate, and restart when a thread drifts.
Resetting all memory to fix one wrong detail is too broad, and the per-chat memory switch must be set before the first message.
lessons.scenario: An operations team uses Claude for three jobs. Each night it tags 800 expense lines by category on a small, fast model at low effort, checked by sampling. Each Monday it writes a candidate update from the same rubric and job descriptions, which live in a Project so nobody re-pastes them. Once a quarter an analyst compares four vendors using public information and internal documents from a connected drive, so she turns on research mode with web search enabled and accepts the wait. When a long vendor chat gets cluttered, she asks for a handoff summary, corrects it and starts fresh.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a one-page decision guide for your team: task type, feature, model tier, effort. Revisit it when a new model ships, because the lineup and settings change. Watch usage: if limits run out early, look for routine tasks running at heavy settings. Check what your plan and administrators allow before promising a stakeholder a workflow that depends on research or retrieval. When a result disappoints, ask whether the cause is the model or the prompt; improving the request is usually cheaper than moving up a tier.

lessons.title: Designing, Integrating and Explaining Claude-Assisted Workflows
lessons.summary: How to use Claude to analyze requirements and use cases, support research, planning and process improvement, prototype and iterate on solutions, fit Claude into an existing workflow by augmenting or redesigning it, and explain its value and limits to stakeholders (Domain 4).
lessons.reading:
A workflow is a repeatable chain of steps that turns an input into a result: interview notes into a requirements list, customer emails into replies, figures into a report. Start with analysis. When sales asks for 'better lead tracking', paste in your interview notes and have Claude list each requirement with its source, flag conflicts and assumptions, and rewrite vague words such as 'fast' as measurable proposals. The people who own the need still confirm the result. Then judge use-case fit: work that recurs often, is text-heavy, can be checked quickly and costs little if wrong makes a strong first pilot, while decisions about individuals, exact payroll figures and restricted data do not.

Claude can also support research, planning and process improvement, but it knows only what you tell it. For research, state the decision the findings feed and the sources allowed, ask for findings in a table by source and date, then open the sources yourself. Describe how a process really runs, with steps, owners and timings, and ask for a process map and the likely bottleneck, the step where work queues up. Speeding up any other step does not raise output, and Claude's candidate comes from your description, so confirm it with timing data. For plans, give the goal, deadline, team capacity and constraints and ask for a work breakdown structure and a risk register, and run a pre-mortem: assume the launch failed and list why. Compare options in a decision matrix whose weights your stakeholders set.

For solution design, build something small and let people react. Ask Claude for a working prototype as an artifact, such as a shift-coverage calculator, let three colleagues try it and revise where they stumble. Each round is a feedback loop. Anything that must connect to company systems, handle sensitive records or run at scale is a technical implementation: describe the problem, the data and your prototype, and escalate it to Claude Developers or Architects.

To integrate Claude, choose an integration point, one step with a defined input, output and receiver. Anthropic's AI Fluency framework names three modes: automation, where Claude carries out a task you define; augmentation, where you and Claude work as thinking partners and you decide; and agency, where Claude is set up in advance to act for you and needs the clearest limits. Most Associate work follows the draft-review-approve pattern: Claude drafts a reply from the ticket and approved answers, the agent edits it, and only then is it sent. If a step exists only because of an old limit, such as retyping handwritten notes, redesign the workflow rather than bolting Claude on. Record a short standard operating procedure: inputs, instructions, reviewer, destination and failure handling.

Stakeholders will ask whether it works, so bring evidence. Record a baseline first, such as minutes per report and corrections needed, run a pilot with a small group and compare. A value case states the measured gain, the cost, the known limits and the review that stays with people. Set expectations early: Claude can state inaccurate specifics and knows only what you tell it. Widen access in stages (gradual release) and plan for adoption with training, a named owner and a place to report problems.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to workflow design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen that hires a fast, tireless prep cook who has never seen your menu. You would not hand over the whole dinner service on day one. You would decide which station suits the newcomer, write down the recipe, taste each dish before it leaves the pass, try them on one quiet shift and compare the numbers with the week before. Adding Claude to a team process works the same way: pick the step, give clear instructions, keep a person checking the result, pilot it small and measure against what you had.
commonTraps: Claude's lists of requirements, bottlenecks and risks are hypotheses built from what you told it, so stakeholders and real data must confirm them.
Speeding up a step that is not the bottleneck changes little, and changing several things at once makes it impossible to tell what helped.
Dropping the review stage after a good first week turns assistance into unchecked automation; relax controls in stages and never where errors are costly.
Connections to company systems, authentication, sensitive records or scale are for Claude Developers and Architects, who need your clear problem statement rather than a finished build.
A value case resting on Claude's own time estimate, one impressive example or login counts is weaker than measured results against a baseline recorded before the pilot.
lessons.scenario: An operations analyst at a regional retail chain spends two days each month turning store managers' emails into a performance summary for executives. She asks Claude to turn a sample of the emails into a table of each store's issue, the evidence given and the owner, flagging gaps. She maps the current process, notices that chasing late emails takes longer than the writing, and has Claude draft a reminder template. After a four-week pilot in two regions she shows the executives the time per summary and the corrections needed before and after, plus two errors that review caught and how they were fixed.
lessons.onTheJob: Start small and keep score. Pick one step, write down today's numbers before you change anything, and keep a short log of what you changed and what happened. Ask Claude for hypotheses, then go and check them with the people who do the work. When you present, lead with measured results and say plainly where Claude needed correcting and which reviews stay with people; that candor keeps a sponsor's trust after the first visible mistake. When a request involves company systems, credentials or customer records at scale, stop prototyping and hand specialists a one-page problem statement with your evidence.

lessons.title: Configuring Projects, Instructions and Connected Knowledge
lessons.summary: How to configure Projects with instructions and knowledge sources, write effective standing instructions, manage uploaded files and connectors such as Google Drive and Gmail, and keep configurations current, tested and trusted (Domain 5).
lessons.reading:
Claude offers several places to store what it should know and how it should behave. Account-wide instructions (Settings, 'Instructions for Claude') apply to every conversation, so keep them for preferences true everywhere, such as defining acronyms. A Project is a workspace with its own chats, instructions and knowledge: project instructions apply to every chat in that Project and nowhere else, and project knowledge is the files and text Claude can draw on in each of those chats. A skill is a procedure Claude loads on demand. Two traps: Claude cannot see a Project's name or description, so a rule typed there is ignored, and one chat's context is not shared with the others unless it goes into the instructions or knowledge.

Keep behavior and reference material apart: instructions say how to act, while knowledge says what is true and can be replaced without touching the rules. A support team's instructions might read: 'You draft replies for non-technical retail customers. Keep them under 150 words and quote the relevant section of the refund policy file. If the policy does not cover the question, say so and suggest asking a team lead.' The last sentence is a fallback instruction: it stops Claude guessing when the knowledge is silent. Keep rules consistent, say what to do as well as what to avoid, explain why, skip the shouting, and never put passwords or API keys in instructions.

Claude cannot tell that a file is outdated, so if last year's and this year's leave policy both sit in the Project, it may quote either. Keep a single source of truth: one approved version of each document, replaced when it changes, with a descriptive name such as 'Leave policy 2026-07'. On paid plans, when stored knowledge nears the context limit, retrieval switches on automatically and an indicator appears: Claude searches for the relevant passages instead of holding everything in view, and clear file names and naming the document in your question help it. A Google Doc added from Drive stays synced with the live file; an uploaded file is a static copy.

A connector links Claude to a service such as Google Drive or Gmail. Claude inherits the signed-in person's permissions, so it cannot open a folder you cannot open; if it cannot find a file, check your own access first. On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner enables a connector for the organization, which makes it available but grants nobody access: each person normally signs in with their own account. Owners can set actions to run freely, need approval or be blocked, which only narrows what the service allows; read what Claude proposes before approving a send or share. Custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic, so add connectors, skills and plugins only from sources you trust, since a bad one can expose data.

Name an owner for each shared Project or skill, give Can edit only to maintainers and Can view to everyone else, and keep a change log of what changed, who changed it, when and why. Before editing instructions, keep a regression test set, a handful of representative and tricky requests with notes on good answers, and run it before and after, changing one thing at a time. Tell users what changed, and review on a schedule, retiring stale files and unneeded connectors and shares.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Projects and connectors? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine hiring a temp for a department. The briefing you give on day one ('our customers are retailers, keep replies short, pass refund disputes to a team lead') is the instructions. The binder of policies on the desk is the knowledge. The temp's building badge decides which rooms they can enter, which is how a connector works: it opens only the doors the signed-in person is allowed through. If the binder holds last year's policy next to this year's, the temp may follow either, so someone has to keep the binder current and tell the temp what changed.
commonTraps: A Project's name and description are not visible to Claude, so standing rules written there are never applied; they belong in the project instructions.
Account-wide instructions apply to every conversation, so client- or task-specific rules placed there leak into unrelated work.
Enabling a connector for the organization grants no one access, and no setting can give Claude more than the signed-in person can already open.
Leaving old and new versions of a document in a Project invites Claude to quote either; an instruction to prefer the newest does not replace removing the stale copy.
Changing several rules at once, with no test requests and no log, makes it impossible to tell which change caused a problem.
lessons.scenario: A training manager sets up a Project for her team of eight to draft answers to client questions about the company's services. She uploads the current service guide and pricing sheet as knowledge, and writes instructions that name the readers, set a 150-word limit, require a quote from the service guide, and tell Claude to say so and route the question to her when the guide is silent. She gives two colleagues Can edit and everyone else Can view. When prices change in the spring, she replaces the pricing file instead of adding a second copy, reruns ten saved test questions, notes the change in a log and posts a two-line update to the team.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat a shared Project like a small product with an owner. Keep a page that states the Project's purpose, a list of the files with their dates, and about ten test questions, including two that the knowledge cannot answer. When behavior shifts, check the log first. Try changes in a private test Project where you can. Before connecting a new service or installing a skill, ask who published it, what it can reach and whether the Owner has approved it, and remove access when the task ends. If a rule keeps being ignored, it is usually in the wrong place, vague, or contradicted by another rule.

lessons.title: Protecting Sensitive Data: Privacy, Regulation and Approved Tools
lessons.summary: How to decide what may go into Claude and in what form: data classification, personal and regulated information, approved tools and accounts, minimization and masking, privacy terms and agreements, and what to do when something goes wrong. Covers Domain 6, applying data sensitivity, regulatory and privacy considerations.
lessons.reading:
