Claude only sees what you give it, and what happens to that data depends on the account, the plan, the settings and your employer's rules. So ask first: what kind of data is this? Organizations sort information into tiers, called data classification: public, internal, confidential and restricted. A press release is public; unreleased financials, client contracts and source code are confidential. Some data needs extra care: personally identifiable information (PII), such as a name with an ID or account number; protected health information (PHI), health data tied to a person and regulated in the United States under HIPAA; and credentials such as passwords and API keys, which never belong in a prompt, Project instructions or a knowledge file.

Next ask: which tool and which account? An approved tool list names the tools and plans vetted for work data. Using a personal account for work, called shadow AI, is a problem even with good intentions: nobody has vetted its terms. On individual plans (Free, Pro and Max) a model-improvement setting controls whether chats may be used to improve Claude, and incognito chats are excluded. On Team, Enterprise and the API, inputs and outputs are not used for training by default. None of this decides what you may share: a vendor's training promise is not permission under your own rules or a client contract, and incognito does not switch your policy off.

Then shrink the exposure. Data minimization means sending only what the task needs: to find which departments log the most overtime, send only department and weekly hours and leave names and ID numbers behind. Redaction blacks out details in a document, but identifiers can survive in file names, headers, comments and tracked changes, so check them. Pseudonymization swaps identifiers for consistent codes (E-017 instead of a name) so rows still match while the key is kept elsewhere; because the key allows re-identification, the data may still count as personal data. Anonymization is stricter: nobody can be identified even by combining the data with other facts, which fails when rare titles, dates or places remain.

Regulation and contracts add rules. The EU's GDPR requires a lawful basis, data minimization and respect for individuals' rights. HIPAA requires a business associate agreement (BAA) and a covered setup before a vendor handles PHI; Anthropic offers a BAA for HIPAA-ready commercial services, not for individual plans. A data processing addendum (DPA) governs how a vendor handles personal data for you and is part of Anthropic's commercial terms. Certifications such as SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 are useful evidence in a vendor risk assessment but do not make your own use lawful. Your privacy or legal team decides.

Plan for mistakes. Deleting a chat clears it from your history at once, but back-end deletion follows later, so it does not undo a disclosure: report it promptly through your escalation path. Connectors work through your own permissions, and a chat share link shows the whole conversation, so read it before sharing. Files and web pages from unknown sources can hide instructions meant to hijack Claude (prompt injection): keep sensitive connections out of such chats and stop Claude if it does something you did not ask for.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to data protection? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of Claude as a capable contractor you invite into a room. You would not hand over the whole filing cabinet; you would bring only the folders the job needs, with names covered if they are not needed, and you would use the contractor your company has already vetted, not one a friend recommended. If a folder went in by mistake, you would tell your manager the same day instead of hoping nobody noticed.
commonTraps: A vendor's promise not to train on your data is not permission to share it; company rules and client contracts still decide what may be pasted.
Removing names is not anonymization: coded data with a key is only pseudonymized, and rare titles, dates and places can still identify people.
Incognito chats and the model-improvement setting change how Claude stores or uses a chat, not what your employer allows you to share.
Telling Claude to ignore or forget data does not undo sharing it; minimize before sending and report mistakes.
Certifications such as SOC 2 or ISO support a vendor review but do not make your own use of a tool lawful.
lessons.scenario: A people-analytics coordinator is asked which departments log the most overtime. The payroll export has names, home addresses, national ID numbers, department and weekly hours. She checks the AI policy, which restricts personal data in AI tools, opens the company's approved Claude workspace and keeps only the department and hours columns. Before uploading she checks the file name and the spreadsheet's other tabs for stray identifiers, and afterwards she notes in the team log what she used and who reviewed the result.
lessons.onTheJob: Build the habit of asking three questions before every upload: what is this data, is this the approved place for it, and what is the least I can send? Keep a short list of safe patterns, such as department-level summaries or coded IDs, so colleagues do not reinvent them. Never fix a privacy slip quietly: a same-day report to the privacy or security team is almost always the cheapest outcome. When your policy is silent, ask its owner instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Appropriate Use, Company Policy and Responsible Practice
lessons.summary: How to judge whether a use of Claude is appropriate, what Anthropic's Usage Policy and an organization's AI policy require, and how bias, transparency, accountability and human oversight apply to everyday work. Covers Domain 6: appropriate and inappropriate use cases, organizational AI policies and governance standards, and the ethical implications of AI use.
lessons.reading:
Not every use of Claude carries the same risk, and the first skill is sorting them. An assistive use supports your own work, such as drafting, summarizing, brainstorming or analyzing while a person reads the result, and an imperfect output does little harm. A high-risk use feeds advice or decisions that can significantly affect someone's rights, health, money or opportunities. Anthropic's Usage Policy names areas such as legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and public benefits. For these it asks that a qualified person meaningfully review the recommendation, with authority to change it, and that the affected person be clearly told that AI was used. Risk grows as output moves from informing a person to deciding about one.

'Meaningful' is the key word. A reviewer with ten seconds, who sees only the AI's summary and cannot overrule it, is a rubber stamp, and automation bias, the habit of trusting a machine's answer, does the rest. Real review needs time, the source documents and authority. The same logic gives the professional-advice boundary: Claude can explain a clause or prepare your questions, but a lawyer, doctor or accountant gives the advice you act on. Some uses are simply out of bounds. The Usage Policy prohibits deceptive content such as fake reviews, invented testimonials, undisclosed fake personas and bots that claim to be human, along with discrimination on protected attributes. Consumer-facing chatbots must say they are AI, and people who deploy agents answer for what those agents do.

Ethics shows up in ordinary choices. Bias can enter through criteria that look neutral: a shortlist rule favoring 'recent graduates' can screen out older candidates without ever mentioning age, a pattern called disparate impact. The remedy is to compare outcomes by group, involve HR or legal and keep a person accountable, not to ask Claude to be fair. Transparency means telling clients, customers and applicants where AI helped when contracts, policy or law expect it. A watermark can signal that Claude produced text, but editing can remove it, so a missing mark never proves that a person wrote it. Accountability stays with you; Anthropic's AI Fluency framework calls it Diligence: take responsibility for what you do with AI, be open about its role and verify before you share.

Your organization's AI acceptable use policy turns these principles into rules: approved tools and accounts, which data is allowed where, which tasks need review or disclosure, and whom to ask. Anthropic's Usage Policy is the outer limit. Your employer may be stricter, and then the stricter rule applies to you. When the policy is silent, ask its owner; silence is not permission. A new plugin or connector gets a vendor risk assessment before real data touches it. Apply least privilege to Project sharing and connectors, keep an audit trail (tool, date, purpose, reviewer, edits) where work is regulated, and use the escalation path quickly when output looks wrong, data went somewhere it should not, or a rule is unclear.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to responsible AI use? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Consider how a hospital treats a new assistant. Taking notes and preparing a draft summary is fine; deciding who receives treatment is not, and every decision that affects a patient is checked by a licensed clinician who can overrule the assistant and who tells the patient what happened. The hospital also has rules about which systems may hold patient files and a person to call when something looks wrong. Responsible use of Claude follows the same pattern: help freely with the preparing, keep qualified people in charge of the deciding, tell people when it matters, and know whom to ask.
commonTraps: Seeing a person click 'approve' is not meaningful review; the reviewer needs time, information and the authority to change the result.
A neutral-sounding criterion can still discriminate through proxies, so removing one field or asking Claude to be unbiased does not settle bias.
A use that Anthropic's Usage Policy allows may still be forbidden by your employer, and silence in your policy is not permission.
A friendly persona is fine, but a consumer-facing chatbot that claims to be human, or reviews written by no customer, is deceptive.
A missing AI watermark does not show that a person wrote the text.
lessons.scenario: A hiring manager wants Claude to rank 400 applications and send automatic rejections to the bottom half. The HR lead explains that employment is a high-risk area, so Claude is used only to summarize each application against the posted requirements. Recruiters read the summaries and the originals and make every decision themselves, and the application form tells candidates that AI supports screening. After the first round the team compares the shortlist by age group and gender, finds a gap, rewrites one criterion and logs the change.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat the policy as a starting point, not a hurdle. Learn where your organization's AI policy lives and who owns it before you need it. When you design a workflow, mark each step as assistive or decision-making, and give the second kind a named reviewer with the authority to overrule. Keep a one-line log of what AI contributed. If something might harm a person, or is something you would not want to explain to a customer or regulator, escalate before you proceed.

lessons.title: Fixing Weak Outputs and Optimizing Your Workflow
lessons.summary: A method for diagnosing why Claude's output falls short, changing one thing at a time, knowing when to switch approach or escalate, and tuning a workflow for speed, cost and quality. Covers Domain 7: diagnosing and resolving underperforming prompts and poor outputs, adjusting approach from feedback and results, and optimizing workflows.
lessons.reading:
When an output disappoints, resist rewording at random. Work backwards: name the symptom, guess the likeliest cause, change one thing, retest. A generic answer means missing context: the audience, the purpose, the quality bar and an example of the voice you want. The wrong shape means the format was never specified, so describe the layout positively and show a sample. A rule that gets skipped is often buried in a long prompt, phrased only as a prohibition, or in conflict with another rule, such as 'keep every answer to two sentences' beside 'explain your reasoning in full'. Different results on each run usually mean the request leaves terms and layout open: define the labels, fix the layout and add examples.

Some problems are not about wording. If Claude lacks the facts, such as your company's headcount or news after its training cutoff, no rewording helps: attach or connect the material, or use search, and have Claude answer only from it. In a long chat early rules drift out of focus, so restate them, or start a fresh chat from a short checked summary and move standing rules into Project instructions. A reply cut off midway can be continued by giving Claude the original request and the part so far. Product messages have their own remedies: 'Your message will exceed the length limit' means split the document or select the relevant parts, a capacity message means wait a few minutes and retry, and a reconnect prompt on a connector means sign in again and check your access. If Claude declines a request it misread, state your legitimate purpose and audience; if the request conflicts with policy, respect the limit and ask for a legitimate alternative.

Iterate with evidence. Keep a small test set of real examples, including messy ones with empty fields and odd formats. Change one element, rerun the same examples and compare against the same criteria; change six at once and you will not know what worked. To compare two prompts, give both the same inputs. Keep dated versions with a note on what changed, so a 'fix' that made things worse can be undone, and save the winning prompt as a template, Project instruction or skill right away. Watch for diminishing returns: when several rounds barely move the result, the obstacle lies elsewhere. Change approach: search for current facts, a Project for recurring context, a smaller step or a person; hand technical work, such as exact matching across thousands of rows, to a developer.

Optimizing a workflow means effectiveness as well as speed. Measure cycle time (the whole loop, including review) and rework rate against a baseline from before Claude: a draft that is rewritten half the time saves little. Find the bottleneck; if drafting takes five minutes and approval takes three days, faster drafting changes little. Feed reviewers' corrections back into the instructions so the same fix is not made by hand every week. To stretch your usage, batch related questions in one message, refer back to earlier material instead of repeating it, keep recurring documents in a Project (reused content counts less while it is fresh) and match the model and effort to the task. Keep human checkpoints where mistakes would be costly or hard to undo; removing them for speed is over-automation.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to troubleshooting AI output? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine a recipe that keeps coming out wrong. A good cook does not throw in random new ingredients. They notice the symptom (too dry), think of the likeliest cause (oven too hot), change one thing and taste again, then write the winning version on a card. If the dish needs an ingredient the kitchen does not have, no amount of stirring helps, and if it needs a pastry chef's skill, they call one. Fixing Claude's output works the same way.
commonTraps: Rewording cannot supply facts Claude does not have; a knowledge gap needs the material, not a cleverer prompt.
Changing many things at once, or asking Claude which edit helped, hides the cause; change one thing and rerun the same test examples.
Retrying an oversized message, or rewriting a prompt after a capacity message, treats the wrong problem; match the fix to the message.
A faster first draft is not a better workflow if reviewers rewrite most of it; measure cycle time and rework rate against a baseline.
A declined request that truly conflicts with policy is a limit, not a puzzle; disguising it is never troubleshooting.
lessons.scenario: A support team's saved prompt drafts replies to customers. Agents report that the drafts sound cold with upset customers and that the layout differs from agent to agent. The team collects ten real examples, adds a short sample reply for upset customers and a fixed three-part layout, and reruns the same ten examples to compare the results. The warmer drafts now need fewer edits. Billing replies are accepted unchanged most of the time, while technical replies still miss details, so the team adds the product guides to its Project and routes technical drafts to a specialist.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a troubleshooting log: symptom, suspected cause, change made, result. After a few weeks it becomes your own playbook. Set a limit on iterations, say three or four rounds, and when you reach it change approach or ask for help instead of polishing wording. Save every prompt that works, with a sample of good output, where teammates can find it. And measure what matters: if the review step is where the time goes, fix that step.

cheatSheet.heading: Prompting essentials (Domain 1)
points: Claude knows only what is in the conversation: give background (purpose, reader, situation), a direct task, the output format and constraints.
Colleague test: if a coworker with no context would be confused by the request, Claude will be too.
Say what to do ("write three short paragraphs") rather than only what to avoid, and explain why a rule exists so Claude can generalize it.
Examples steer format and tone best: one is a start, three to five give consistency; make them relevant, diverse and clearly labeled as examples.
Label pasted material (Notes:, Template:, Instructions:). With long documents put the document first and the question last.
Files: PDFs up to 100 pages are read for text and visuals, longer PDFs as text only; non-PDF files give text only, so embedded images are not read. Say which file and which part you mean.
A role helps only if it names a perspective and what it cares about. Save prompts that work as templates with placeholders.

cheatSheet.heading: Decomposition, iteration and task types
points: Task decomposition splits a big job into stages with one purpose each. Prompt chaining feeds each output into the next so you can inspect it; it trades speed for accuracy and control.
Self-correction chain: draft, review against criteria you state, refine. Number the steps when order matters.
Iterate deliberately: set success criteria first, judge the output against them, give targeted feedback (keep this, change that), and change one thing at a time.
Start simple and add rules only for observed problems. A bloated, contradictory prompt gets worse; cut back to a core request.

Analysis: data plus question plus the decision it feeds, and ask for method and assumptions. Research: success criteria, cross-check sources, flag conflicts, give links. Drafting: reader, purpose, tone, length, voice samples. Brainstorming: many varied options first, narrow later with criteria.
For an ambiguous request invite clarifying questions. For hard multi-constraint reasoning ask for step-by-step work or use extended thinking, then check the result.

cheatSheet.heading: Hallucinations and validation (Domain 2)
points: Hallucination: fluent, confident, false or unsupported content such as invented statistics, quotes, citations and clause numbers. Techniques reduce it; none eliminates it.
Not verification: a confident tone, "are you sure?", self-rated confidence, rerunning and getting the same answer, or Claude vouching for its own citations.
Verification: the primary source, independent recalculation, a second reliable source, opening every cited link and judging its credibility and date, and expert review.

Prompt techniques: allow "I don't know"; quote-first for long documents; restrict to supplied material; ask for a supporting passage per claim and drop the unsupported; compare several runs; read the thinking summary when an answer looks wrong.

Failure shapes: fabricated details, knowledge cutoff (needs web search or a document), inconsistency, omissions, claimed actions that never happened (confirm in the real app), broken links, arithmetic slips.
Accuracy means what is stated is right; completeness means everything required is present. Use a requirements checklist, and spot-check a sample plus ambiguous cases for big outputs.

cheatSheet.heading: Human review, bias, audiences and formats (Domain 2)
points: Scale checking to stakes. High-stakes content (legal, financial, medical, safety, regulatory, decisions about individuals) needs qualified human review, and the sender stays accountable. Beware automation bias.

Bias shows up as stereotypes, one-sided framing, omissions and sycophancy. Checks: counterfactual swap test, request multiple perspectives and counterarguments, neutral wording instead of leading questions, expert review.

Audience adaptation: name the reader, the need and the length, then recheck against the original for meaning drift. Use targeted revision for one passage, compare variants against criteria, and edit an earlier message to branch.
Curate and synthesize with criteria: group by theme, tabulate claims by source, flag conflicts and gaps.

Formats: inline for short answers; an artifact for substantial, editable, shareable content (private until shared); structured data (fixed-column table or CSV) for spreadsheets; created files (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF) need code execution and file creation on, and review.

cheatSheet.heading: Products, models and context (Domain 3)
points: Feature choice: chat is the default; web search for quick current facts with citations; extended thinking for harder reasoning (no new information); research for a multi-source cited report (minutes, paid plans, needs web search on, uses allowance faster); a Project for recurring work with shared files and instructions; an artifact for substantial editable output or a small interactive tool.

Models: Haiku is fastest and cheapest (classification, extraction, high volume); Sonnet is the balanced default; Opus is high capability for demanding work; Fable sits above Opus as the most capable, slowest and costliest. Start small and move up, or start strong where accuracy outweighs cost.
Effort runs low to max: higher is more thorough, slower and uses limits faster. Thinking is a separate control. Model, effort and thinking can change mid-chat and apply from the next response.

The context window is working memory counted in tokens; more is not better (context rot). Paid plans with code execution on summarize long chats automatically; restart with a corrected handoff summary when a thread drifts.

Keep stable material in a Project, where retrieval brings in relevant parts when knowledge is large. Chat memory saves editable topics (Settings > Memory) and each Project has its own; switch memory off before the first message of a sensitive or unrelated chat, and edit or delete a topic rather than reset everything.
Plan and administrator settings decide what you have (research needs a paid plan and web search on), so check before designing a workflow around a feature.

cheatSheet.heading: Workflow integration and solution design (Domain 4)
points: Analyze before you build: give Claude interview notes and ask for requirements with sources, conflicts and assumptions, plus an ambiguity check that turns words like 'fast' into measurable targets. Stakeholders confirm; Claude only drafts.

Use-case fit: frequent, text-heavy, easy-to-check, low-consequence work with data you may share is a strong first pilot. Decisions about individuals, exact payroll or legal figures and restricted data are poor fits. Rank ideas by impact versus effort, using criteria the team sets.

Process work: map the real steps (owner, input, output), find the bottleneck, confirm it with timing data, change one thing at a time and compare with the baseline. Speeding up a step that is not the bottleneck changes little.

Planning aids Claude can draft from facts you supply: work breakdown structure, risk register, pre-mortem (assume failure, list the causes), assumption log, gap analysis (needs both today's state and the target state) and decision matrix (people set the weights).

Prototype in an artifact, let users try it and iterate on their feedback. Anything needing company-system integration, authentication, sensitive records or scale is escalated to Claude Developers or Architects with a clear problem statement.

Modes (AI Fluency): automation = Claude executes a task you define; augmentation = thinking partners, the person decides; agency = configured in advance to act independently, which needs the clearest limits. Most Associate work is augmentation.

Integrate at one integration point with a defined input, output and receiver. Draft-review-approve keeps a person accountable. Redesign, not an add-on, when a step exists only because of an old limit such as retyping notes. Write an SOP: inputs, instructions or template, reviewer, destination and failure handling.

Prove and explain value: record a baseline, run a pilot, compare, then present a value case with measured gain, cost, limits and the review that stays. Avoid Claude's own estimates, one best example and activity counts. Set expectations early, release gradually and plan for adoption (training, an owner, a feedback channel).

cheatSheet.heading: Projects, instructions and knowledge (Domain 5)
points: Where things live: account-wide instructions ('Instructions for Claude' in Settings) apply to every conversation; project instructions apply to all chats in that Project only; project knowledge is reference material for every chat in that Project; skills load on demand when a request matches.

Claude cannot see a Project's name or description, so rules written there are ignored. Context from one chat is not shared with the other chats in a Project unless it is added to the knowledge or instructions.

Instructions = behavior (role and audience, tone, format, source rule, fallback). Knowledge = facts and documents. Do not paste documents into instructions or bury rules in a document; keep volatile facts such as prices in a replaceable knowledge file.

Effective instructions are specific and consistent, explain why, say what to do, name the audience, require a quote from the source and include a fallback for missing information (say so, name who to ask). Use normal wording rather than shouting, and never include passwords or API keys.

Knowledge hygiene: a single source of truth, one approved version per document, descriptive names with dates or versions, superseded files retired, and a scheduled review. Claude cannot tell that a file is outdated, and an instruction to 'prefer the newest' does not replace removing the stale copy.

Retrieval (RAG) on paid plans switches on automatically as knowledge nears the context limit, with a visual indicator, so a Project can hold far more material. Help it with descriptive names, related files kept together, and the document named in the question.
Sharing (Team and Enterprise): Can view lets members read the Project and chat in it; Can edit lets them change its instructions and knowledge. Give edit rights only to the maintainers.

cheatSheet.heading: Connectors, skills and keeping configurations healthy (Domain 5)
points: Connectors link Claude to services such as Google Drive and Gmail. Claude inherits the signed-in person's permissions and cannot reach what that person cannot open; if a file is missing, check the person's own access first.

On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner enables a connector (available, but no one gets access by that step) and each person normally signs in with their own account. Owner permission levels (allow, needs approval, blocked) can only narrow access. Read each proposed action before approving it.

A Google Doc added from Drive stays synced with the live file; an uploaded file is a static copy. The Drive connector reads text only, so images inside documents are not seen. Enterprise search is a permission-aware project that searches connected tools for each person.

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources loaded by progressive disclosure: name and description first, full content only when relevant, so the description decides whether a skill is used. Try several sample prompts and sharpen the description if it does not trigger. Build one when you keep re-explaining the same format. A plugin bundles skills and connectors.

Trusted-source rule: add connectors, skills and plugins only from sources you trust and need. Custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic, and untrusted skills risk prompt injection and data exfiltration, so review the contents first.

Maintain: a named configuration owner; edit rights for maintainers only; a change log (what, who, when, why); a regression test set run before and after each change, one change at a time; tell users what changed; and an access review that removes unused connectors and shares.

cheatSheet.heading: Appropriate use and responsible practice (Domain 6)
points: Assistive uses (drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, analysis for your own work, with a person reading the result) are the safe place to start. Risk rises as output moves from informing a person to deciding about one.

High-risk areas include legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and public benefits. Anthropic's Usage Policy asks for meaningful review by a qualified person who can change the result, and for affected people to be clearly told that AI was used.
Meaningful review needs time, the source documents and authority to overrule. A rubber stamp is not review, and automation bias is the habit of trusting a machine's answer.

Out of bounds under the Usage Policy: deceptive content (fake reviews, invented testimonials, undisclosed personas, bots claiming to be human), discrimination on protected attributes, and collecting sensitive data without permission. Consumer-facing chatbots must say they are AI, and users answer for agents they deploy.
Professional-advice boundary: Claude explains and prepares; a licensed professional advises and carries the responsibility.
Bias and disparate impact: neutral-looking criteria can act as proxies. Compare outcomes by group, involve HR or legal and keep a person accountable; asking Claude to be fair is not a control.

Transparency and accountability (AI Fluency: Diligence): be open about AI's role where policy, contracts or law expect it, verify before you share, and own what you send. A watermark is a signal, and a missing mark never proves human authorship.

cheatSheet.heading: Data sensitivity, privacy and company policy (Domain 6)
points: Three questions before any upload: what is the data (public, internal, confidential or restricted; PII, PHI, credentials), is this the approved tool and account, and what is the least I can send?

Minimize first, then redact or pseudonymize. Check the file name, headers, comments, tracked changes and properties. Coded data with a key is only pseudonymized and may still be personal data; anonymized data cannot be traced back even when combined with other facts.
Credentials never go into prompts, Project instructions, knowledge files or skills.

Individual plans (Free, Pro, Max) have a model-improvement setting; on Team, Enterprise and the API, inputs and outputs are not used for training by default. Incognito chats are excluded from improvement. None of this replaces company rules, and a personal account used for work is shadow AI.

Agreements and standards: a DPA covers processing of personal data; a BAA covers PHI (HIPAA-ready commercial services only, not individual plans); GDPR governs EU personal data and the privacy team decides. SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 support a vendor risk assessment but do not make your use lawful.

The AI acceptable use policy (approved tools, data, review, disclosure) can be stricter than the Usage Policy, and silence is not permission: ask its owner. Vendor risk assessment before new plugins or connectors; least privilege for sharing and connectors; audit trail for regulated work.

When it goes wrong: deleting a chat clears your history at once but back-end deletion lags, so report promptly through the escalation path. Untrusted files and pages can hide instructions (prompt injection), so stop unexpected actions. Read a chat's whole conversation before sharing its link.

cheatSheet.heading: Troubleshooting and optimization (Domain 7)
points: Diagnose before changing: name the symptom, find the likeliest cause, change one thing, retest on the same examples.

Symptom to cause: generic means missing context; wrong shape means no format shown; a skipped rule is buried, negative or conflicting; varying results mean undefined terms and an open layout; invented facts mean a knowledge gap; early rules fading in a long chat is drift; too brief means undefined depth.

Fixes: supply the material and answer only from it; show the layout and examples; settle conflicts with a priority; restart from a short checked summary and keep standing rules in Project instructions; define the depth wanted; continue a cut-off reply by giving the original request and the part so far.

Not always the prompt: a length-limit notice means split the file or select parts; a capacity message means wait and retry, and check the status page if it persists; a reconnect prompt means sign in again and check access. A misread refusal needs the purpose stated; a real policy conflict is a limit, never to be disguised.

Iterate with evidence: a test set with messy cases, the same inputs for A/B comparisons, dated prompt versions, and winners saved as templates, Project instructions or skills. Diminishing returns means change approach (another feature or source, a smaller step, a person) or escalate technical work.

Optimize the whole loop: compare cycle time and rework rate with a baseline, fix the bottleneck, feed reviewer corrections back into the instructions, batch related questions, refer back instead of repeating, keep recurring documents in a Project (reused content counts less while fresh), and match model and effort to the task.
Keep human checkpoints where errors are costly or hard to reverse; removing them for speed is over-automation.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 60 items, multiple choice and multiple response (each item states how many to select), 120 minutes, proctored through Pearson VUE online or at a test center. That is about two minutes an item, so flag hard items and return.
Scoring: scaled 100-1,000 with a pass at 720, measured against a fixed standard rather than other candidates. The report shows percent correct by domain, but pass or fail depends on the total.

Weights: Prompting 14, Output evaluation 21, Product and model selection 12, Workflow integration 16, Configuration and knowledge 12, Governance 15, Troubleshooting 10. Output evaluation is the largest domain, so practice verification judgments.

Items are workplace scenarios asking for the best or most appropriate action, not code. Pick the answer that matches the principle: verify against a primary source, match model and effort to the task, give context and structure, keep a human in the loop for high stakes, and escalate technical work.

Eliminate the usual wrong answers: trusting confident output or self-rated confidence, using the biggest model for everything, over-engineering a simple task, uploading sensitive data as-is, vague prompts and skipped review.
Read the stem for constraints (speed, cost, stakes, audience, data sensitivity) and for "choose two" or "choose three", then select exactly that many.
Logistics: $99 fee, valid government photo ID matching your registration, credential valid 12 months, retake waits of 14, 30 and 90 days, up to four attempts in a rolling year.

madlibs.scenario: A manager's request 'Summarize this report' returns a generic summary. Adding the reader, the purpose and the desired length supplies {b1}, and pasting two sample summaries in the layout she wants adds {b2} that show the format. When the report is very long, she places the document {b3} her question.

options: background context
a role assignment
a chain of steps
examples
delimiters
constraints
before
after
inside

madlibs.explanation: The reader, purpose and length are background context. Sample outputs are examples, one of the most reliable ways to steer format. With long material, Anthropic recommends putting the document first and the question after it.

madlibs.scenario: A project manager splits a big request into stages in which each answer feeds the next. Splitting the job is called {b1}, running the stages as a sequence of requests is called {b2}, and the approach usually trades {b3} for accuracy and control.

options: task decomposition
prompt chaining
role prompting
task decomposition
prompt chaining
few-shot prompting
speed
relevance
privacy

madlibs.explanation: Breaking a job into stages is task decomposition; feeding each output into the next request is prompt chaining. Because several requests take longer than one, chaining trades speed for the ability to inspect and correct each stage.

madlibs.scenario: Claude invents a statistic and attributes it to a report that does not exist; this failure is called a {b1}. Asking Claude to rate its own certainty gives only {b2}, which is not evidence, so the figure should be checked against the {b3}.

options: hallucination
jailbreak
context rot
self-reported confidence
a primary source
a swap test
primary source
chat history
thinking summary

madlibs.explanation: An invented but plausible statement is a hallucination. A confidence rating from Claude is self-reported and is not independent evidence, so the claim is verified against the original (primary) source.

madlibs.scenario: A short clarification belongs {b1} in the chat. A one-page policy template that she will edit, reuse and share suits {b2}. Supplier data to be sorted and filtered in a spreadsheet should be requested as {b3} with fixed columns.

options: inline
in an artifact
in a Project
an artifact
an inline reply
a research report
structured data
flowing prose
a narrative summary

madlibs.explanation: Short answers stay inline. Substantial, self-contained content you will edit and share suits an artifact. Data that will be sorted and filtered needs structured output with defined fields rather than prose.

madlibs.scenario: A quick check of who was named chief executive this week calls for {b1}. A long comparison of four vendors drawing on the web and connected files calls for {b2}. A scheduling puzzle with many conflicting rules, where no outside information is needed, calls for {b3}.

options: web search
research mode
extended thinking
research mode
web search
a standard chat
extended thinking
web search
research mode

madlibs.explanation: Web search handles quick current-fact lookups. Research mode runs many connected searches across the web and enabled integrations and returns a cited report. Extended thinking helps with hard reasoning when everything needed is already in the chat.

madlibs.scenario: The fastest and cheapest tier is {b1}, the balanced middle tier is {b2}, and the high-capability tier for demanding, nuanced work is {b3}. When a long chat drifts, she asks Claude for a {b4} and starts a new conversation.

options: Haiku
Sonnet
Opus
Haiku
Sonnet
Opus
Haiku
Sonnet
Opus
handoff summary
prompt template
swap test

madlibs.explanation: Haiku is the fastest and cheapest tier, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence, and Opus is for demanding work. A handoff summary carries the decisions and open questions into a clean new chat.

madlibs.scenario: Before a team pilots Claude on its weekly client report, the coordinator records how long the report takes and how many corrections it needs; this is a {b1}. In the new workflow Claude writes the first version, an account manager checks and edits it, and only then is it sent, a pattern called {b2}. After the pilot she presents the measured gain, the cost, the known limits and the review that stays with people, which together form the {b3}.

options: regression test set
baseline measurement
risk register
draft-review-approve
gradual release
impact-effort prioritization
assumption log
decision matrix
value case

madlibs.explanation: Recording how long the work takes and how many corrections it needs before Claude is involved gives a baseline measurement, the only fair yardstick for the pilot. Claude drafts, a responsible person reviews, and only then is the work released: the draft-review-approve pattern, whereas gradual release means widening Claude's scope in stages. The measured gain, cost, limits and remaining review form a value case; a decision matrix scores options and an assumption log tracks unproven beliefs.

madlibs.scenario: For one team's reply-drafting Project, the audience, the tone and what to do when the answer is missing are standing rules, so they go in {b1}. The current refund policy is reference material, so it goes in {b2}. A preference that should hold in every conversation a person has, such as spelling out acronyms on first use, belongs in {b3}.

options: the project description
project instructions
project knowledge
project instructions
account-wide instructions
project knowledge
account-wide instructions
project knowledge
a skill

madlibs.explanation: Standing rules about audience, tone and fallback behavior belong in the project instructions; Claude cannot see a Project's description. Reference documents such as a policy belong in project knowledge, where they can be replaced without touching the rules. A preference that is true in every conversation is what account-wide instructions are for, while a skill loads only when a request matches it.

madlibs.scenario: When the leave policy changes, the Project owner replaces the old file instead of adding a second copy, so that the Project keeps a {b1}. The new file is named 'Leave policy 2026-07', a {b2} that helps both people and retrieval pick the right document. Before editing the instructions, she runs a {b3}, a fixed set of representative requests, so that she can see whether answers got worse.

options: single source of truth
separate copy for each team
backup of every earlier version
fallback instruction
descriptive file name
skill description
pre-mortem
gap analysis
regression test set

madlibs.explanation: Replacing the old file rather than adding a copy leaves one approved version, a single source of truth. A name that states the content and date is a descriptive file name. A fixed set of requests rerun before and after a change is a regression test set; a pre-mortem and a gap analysis are planning tools for other jobs.

madlibs.scenario: A project manager wants Claude to find which departments log the most overtime from an export that also holds names and ID numbers. Sending only the columns the task needs is called {b1}. If she swapped the names for consistent codes and stored the key in a separate protected file, the data would be {b2}, which can still count as personal data. Before choosing any tool she should check the company's {b3} to see which AI tools are cleared for work data.

options: data classification
data minimization
pseudonymization
pseudonymized
anonymized
declassified
audit trail
model release notes
approved tool list

madlibs.explanation: Giving Claude only what the task needs is data minimization; classification is the sorting of data into tiers, and pseudonymization is the swapping of identifiers for codes. Coded data whose key still exists is pseudonymized, not anonymized, so re-identification remains possible and it may still be personal data. The approved tool list shows which tools and plans are cleared for work data; an audit trail records how AI was used and release notes describe model changes.

madlibs.scenario: An insurer proposes letting Claude recommend which claims to pay. Because the output would feed a decision about a person's money, this is a {b1} use case, so a qualified person must {b2} each recommendation with the authority to change it, and the affected customer must be {b3}.

options: high-risk
assistive
unrestricted
rubber-stamp
wait for a complaint about
meaningfully review
shown the full chat transcript
told that AI was used
asked to consent to model training

madlibs.explanation: Insurance is one of the high-risk areas in Anthropic's Usage Policy because the output would significantly affect a person's money. Such uses call for meaningful review by a qualified person who can change the result, and for the affected person to be clearly told that AI was used. Assistive uses support your own work; rubber-stamping and reacting to complaints are not review; and a transcript or a training consent is not what the policy asks for.

madlibs.scenario: A team that changes six things at once cannot tell which change helped, so it should change {b1} per round and rerun the same {b2}. When several rounds of edits stop improving the results, it has reached {b3}, so it should change approach or ask a specialist instead of rewording again.

options: every element
one element
the model and the rules
prompt wording
reviewers
test examples
diminishing returns
instruction drift
a knowledge gap

madlibs.explanation: Changing one element per round and rerunning the same test examples isolates what each change does; the wording is the thing being changed, so it cannot be the constant. When several rounds stop paying off the team has hit diminishing returns, which signals that the obstacle is not the wording. Instruction drift describes rules sliding out of focus in a long chat, and a knowledge gap is a cause of poor output, not the name for a plateau.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for iterating on a Claude request in the order they usually occur.
steps: Define success criteria: the reader, what must be covered, the length and the accuracy bar
Write a first prompt with background, the task, the output format and constraints
Run it and read the response against your criteria
Give targeted feedback that names what to keep and what to change
Repeat, changing one thing at a time, until the output meets the criteria
Save the version that worked as a reusable template
sequences.explanation: Criteria come first so you can judge the output. Feedback is specific, and changes are made one at a time so you know what helped. Saving the final prompt as a template makes the result repeatable.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for verifying a long Claude summary before it is shared.
steps: Ask Claude to quote the exact passages behind each claim
Locate those quotes in the source document
Check specific numbers, names, dates and citations against the primary source
Compare the summary with a requirements checklist to find omissions
Fix or remove anything unsupported and recheck any rewritten text
Send high-stakes content for expert sign-off, then share it
sequences.explanation: Quotes make claims traceable, so locating them comes before checking the specifics. Accuracy checks come before the completeness check against the requirements, fixes are rechecked, and human sign-off for high-stakes content is the last gate before sharing.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for validating 500 tickets that Claude classified into the right order.
steps: Define the categories and the error rate you can tolerate
Have Claude classify the tickets
Pull a random sample plus the ambiguous tickets
Compare the sample with your own judgment and estimate the error rate
If the rate is too high, refine the instructions or add examples and rerun
Recheck a fresh sample, then use the results
sequences.explanation: You need a tolerance before you can judge quality. Sampling estimates the error rate cheaply, a poor result sends you back to the instructions rather than to row-by-row repair, and a fresh sample confirms the fix.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for restarting a cluttered long conversation without losing what matters.
steps: Notice that the thread has drifted, collected contradictory instructions or grown too long
Ask Claude for a summary of the decisions, requirements and open questions
Read the summary and correct anything wrong or missing
Open a new chat
Paste the corrected summary as the starting brief and attach any source files again
Continue the work and check that the new chat reflects the summary
sequences.explanation: The summary has to be corrected before it is reused, because errors in it carry into the new chat. Only then is it pasted into a clean conversation, together with the files it depends on.

sequences.prompt: Put the efficiency-first model-selection steps for a recurring task in order.
steps: Write down the quality criteria and the speed and cost limits
Try the task on the smaller, faster model at a modest effort setting
Check the results against the criteria on a realistic sample
If quality falls short, raise the effort or move up a tier
Re-test on the same sample
Standardize on the lightest setting that meets the bar
sequences.explanation: Efficiency-first selection starts light and moves up only where the test shows a gap. Re-testing on the same sample makes the comparison fair, and the final choice is the lightest setting that still meets the criteria.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for bringing Claude into an existing team process in the order they are usually done.
steps: Map how the process works today, with its steps, owners and handoffs
Choose one step that suits Claude and define what goes in, what comes out and who receives it
Record a baseline for that step: the time it takes and how often the output needs correction
Write the instructions or template and decide who reviews the output
Pilot with a small group for a fixed period
Compare the pilot with the baseline, gather feedback and fix what went wrong
Document the procedure and widen access in stages
sequences.explanation: You cannot pick a good integration point until you understand the process. The baseline measures the step you chose, so it follows that choice and must be taken before Claude changes anything. Instructions and the review step are settled before users try the workflow, the pilot is judged against the baseline, and documentation and staged release come last, once the workflow has earned them.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for safely changing the instructions of a shared Project in the order they should happen.
steps: Describe the problem and save a copy of the current instructions
Run the fixed set of test requests on the current version and note the results
Make one change to the instructions
Rerun the same test requests and compare the answers with the notes on good output
Keep the change if results improved and nothing got worse; otherwise revert it
Record the change in the change log and tell users what is different
sequences.explanation: Saving the current version first makes reverting easy, and a run before the change gives you something to compare with. Making one change at a time shows what caused any difference. The decision to keep or revert follows the comparison, and the log entry and user notice come last so that they describe what is actually live.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps for preparing a work file that contains personal data for Claude in the order they usually occur.
steps: Check the data's classification and what your policy allows for it, including which tool and account to use
Remove the columns and records the task does not need
Replace or mask the identifiers that remain, keeping any key separate
Inspect the file name, other sheets, comments and properties for leftover identifiers
Upload the cleaned file in the approved tool and run the task
Review the output before it is shared and record how AI was used
sequences.explanation: Policy comes first because it decides whether the data may be used at all and where. Minimizing before masking leaves less to mask, and the inspection catches identifiers hiding in file names, other tabs and properties before anything leaves your control. Only then is the file uploaded to the approved tool, and the result is reviewed and logged before it is shared.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for fixing a weak Claude output in a workflow you use every week.
steps: Describe the symptom precisely, for example 'the layout changes on every run'
Form a hypothesis about the cause, such as an undefined format
Change one thing to address that cause
Rerun the same test examples and compare the results with the earlier ones
Keep the change if it helped, or revert it and try the next hypothesis
Record the winning version, with a note of what changed, as the new template
sequences.explanation: A precise symptom lets you form a hypothesis, and changing one thing at a time makes the effect visible. Rerunning the same examples keeps the comparison fair, the keep-or-revert decision follows from the evidence, and the winning version is recorded last so the improvement can be repeated and any later change undone.

caseStudies.title: Brightwater Foods: A Vendor Briefing Built with Claude
caseStudies.scenario: Brightwater Foods' procurement team must brief the leadership group on Friday about renewing a contract with a refrigerated-logistics vendor. Priya, an operations analyst on a paid Claude plan, uploads the 45-page contract and asks for a one-page summary of the termination and liability terms. Claude's summary says either party may terminate on 30 days' notice under clause 11.2. Priya also needs a comparison of the vendor with three competitors that draws on public information and on delivery-performance files stored in the company's connected drive, with sources she can check. Finally, the briefing will include a paragraph on the vendor's pending food-safety audit, and the legal team plans to quote that paragraph in a letter to a regulator. Priya wants the briefing in a form she can edit and her manager can comment on. She has one afternoon, so she wants to use Claude where it saves time without letting an unchecked claim reach the leadership group. Her manager has asked that every figure and clause cited in the briefing be traceable to a source.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate way for Priya to treat Claude's statement about the 30-day notice period and clause 11.2?
options: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and keep the statement if the rating is high
Find the clause and notice period in the contract itself and confirm the number and wording
Ask Claude to regenerate the summary and keep the statement if the second version agrees
Accept it, because the summary was produced from the actual contract she uploaded
questions.explanation: A clause number and a notice period are specific details that can be wrong even when the summary reads smoothly, so they are checked against the primary source. Self-rated confidence and a matching second summary are not independent checks, and being derived from the contract does not guarantee a faithful summary.

questions.question: Which setup best fits the vendor comparison?
options: A single web search per competitor, ignoring the internal delivery files
Extended thinking alone, because the comparison needs deep reasoning
Research mode with web search on and the drive connected, then opening the cited sources to check them
A standard chat in which she types what she remembers about each competitor
questions.explanation: Research mode runs many connected searches across the web and enabled integrations and returns a cited report, which fits a multi-source comparison that uses internal files; the citations still need to be opened and checked. Single searches skip the internal files, extended thinking has no access to outside sources, and memory-based input is unverified.

questions.question: Which TWO actions best fit the food-safety paragraph and the briefing format? (Choose two.)
options: Have the legal team or another qualified reviewer check the paragraph against the audit record before it is quoted
Ask Claude to build the briefing as an artifact that Priya can edit and share for comments
Quote the paragraph as Claude wrote it, since it was drafted from sources
Keep the briefing as a chat reply so that nobody else can change it
Ask Claude to confirm that the paragraph is legally sound
questions.explanation: Content that will be quoted to a regulator is high-stakes, so qualified human review is expected before it leaves the building. A substantial document that will be edited and commented on suits an artifact. Drafting from sources does not remove the need for review, a chat reply is hard to edit and share, and Claude confirming its own legal soundness is not a substitute for counsel.

caseStudies.title: Harbour Street Conferences: Faster Quotes with Claude
caseStudies.scenario: Harbour Street Conferences manages meeting venues. Its events team of eight coordinators receives booking requests by email, retypes the details into a tracking sheet and drafts a quote from a price list, and a senior planner checks every quote before it goes to the client. The planner is the only person who knows which discounts are allowed. Coordinators estimate that a quote takes about two hours, and the planner sends roughly one in six back because of pricing mistakes. Lena, the operations lead, has a paid Claude plan and wants quotes produced faster without more errors. The price list is a spreadsheet that finance updates each quarter. The managing director wants a proposal by the end of the month and has asked what Claude can and cannot be trusted with. A senior executive suggests connecting Claude to the booking database so that quotes are generated and emailed to clients the moment a request arrives. Lena has no technical background, and the IT team is small and busy. She has two weeks and four coordinators who are willing to try a new approach.

questions.question: Which design best fits Lena's situation?
options: Claude drafts each quote and emails it straight to the client, and the planner reviews a sample of sent quotes each week
Claude drafts and double-checks each quote itself, so that the planner's review can be dropped to save time
Claude drafts each quote from the request and the price list, a coordinator edits it, and the planner approves it before it is sent
Claude designs a new booking process from scratch and all eight coordinators switch to it at the start of next month
questions.explanation: The draft-review-approve pattern removes the retyping and drafting effort while the planner's check stays where pricing errors are costly. Emailing quotes directly or dropping the planner's review removes the control that now catches roughly one error in six, and Claude cannot know which discounts are allowed. Switching all coordinators to a redesigned process at once skips the pilot that would show whether it works.

questions.question: Which TWO steps will most strengthen Lena's proposal to the managing director? (Choose two.)
options: Ask Claude to estimate the hours the whole team would save and present that figure as the expected result
Time a sample of current quotes and count the returns before the pilot, so that there is a baseline to compare with
Show the three best quotes Claude produced and leave out the ones that needed corrections, to keep the message simple
Pilot with the four coordinators, then report measured time and returns, Claude's mistakes and the checks that stay with people
State that Claude is accurate enough that the planner's review can be dropped once the pilot ends
questions.explanation: The coordinators' two-hour figure is an estimate, not a measurement, so timing a sample and counting returns first creates the baseline that makes any improvement visible. A pilot report that includes Claude's mistakes and the review that remains is what builds credibility. Claude's own savings estimate, hand-picked best examples and a promise that review can be dropped are claims the managing director has no reason to trust.

questions.question: How should Lena respond to the executive's suggestion to connect Claude to the booking database and email quotes automatically?
options: Ask the executive for the database login so that Claude can connect to the booking system during the pilot
Write up the goal, the data involved and the pilot results, and take it to IT or Claude Developers and Architects to design
Decline the idea outright, because Claude cannot be used with the company's booking data in any form
Have Claude write the connection code and put it into use if it runs without errors in testing
questions.explanation: Generating quotes straight from a company database and emailing clients automatically is a technical integration involving authentication, security and reliability, which is beyond Associate scope and belongs with Developers and Architects. Lena's contribution is a clear problem statement and evidence from the pilot. Handing out credentials or deploying untested generated code creates security risk, and refusing outright ignores a legitimate need that specialists can address safely.

caseStudies.title: Larkspur Credit Union: Three AI Requests in One Week
caseStudies.scenario: Larkspur is a regional credit union with about 40,000 members. It has rolled out a company-managed Claude workspace on a commercial plan. Its AI acceptable use policy lists the approved tools, bans account numbers and national ID numbers from any AI tool, and names the compliance office as the contact for questions. Three requests arrive in one week. First, the member-services team wants Claude to find common themes in 2,000 complaint emails, which contain member names, account numbers and free-text descriptions. Second, the lending team proposes that Claude read each hardship-loan application, which includes income and debts, and recommend approve or decline, with loan officers receiving only the recommendation and a one-line reason. Third, a junior analyst, rushed before a board meeting, pasted a list of member account numbers into her personal Claude account to build a chart, then deleted the chat when she remembered the policy. She has told nobody and plans to finish the chart in that account tonight. The compliance office has asked every team to record how Claude was used and who reviewed the results.

questions.question: How should the member-services team prepare the complaint emails for analysis?
options: Upload the emails unchanged, because a company-managed plan does not train on chats by default
Paste a sample of fifty emails into a personal account, since a small sample is low risk
Remove the account numbers, replace names with codes, and work in the approved workspace
Upload the emails unchanged and ask Claude to leave identifying details out of its summary
questions.explanation: The policy bans account numbers from any AI tool, so they come out before the upload, and replacing names with codes lowers the exposure further while the themes can still be found. The approved workspace is the right place, but its training default does not override the policy. A personal account is outside the approved tools whatever the sample size, and asking Claude to leave details out of its summary does not stop them being shared.

questions.question: Which design is most appropriate for the hardship-loan proposal?
options: Claude declines applications automatically when it flags a risk, and officers review only the approvals that remain
Claude approves routine applications automatically, and officers audit a monthly sample of those approvals
Officers receive only the recommendation and a one-line reason, and applicants are not told how it was produced
Officers see the full application, can override the recommendation, and decide each case; applicants are told that AI assists
questions.explanation: Credit is a high-risk area. A qualified person needs the time, the information and the authority to change the outcome, so seeing only a one-line reason is not enough, and the affected applicants must be clearly told that AI was used. Automatic declines or approvals remove that review, and withholding the AI role from applicants breaches the disclosure principle.

questions.question: What should the junior analyst do now? (Choose two.)
options: Tell the compliance office promptly through the escalation route
Say nothing, because deleting the chat removed the account numbers everywhere
Rebuild the chart in the approved workspace, using masked or coded identifiers
Ask Claude to confirm that it has forgotten the account numbers
Wait until after the board meeting to decide whether to raise it
questions.explanation: The disclosure should be reported at once so that compliance can assess and contain it; deleting a chat clears it from your history immediately, but back-end removal follows later, and Claude has no 'forget' control that undoes a disclosure. The chart itself can be finished properly in the approved workspace with masked identifiers. Staying silent, asking Claude for confirmation or delaying the report all leave the company unable to act.

compare.scenario: A sales manager needs Claude to turn messy call notes into a follow-up email to a client who is deciding between two proposals. Which request is the better one?
compare.optionA: Paste the notes under a 'Notes:' label, then give the reader, the decision they face, the tone, a 120-word limit and the next step.
compare.optionB: Paste the notes and ask for a polite, professional follow-up email that summarizes the main points of the call.
compare.why: Claude cannot see who the client is, what they are weighing or what response is wanted, so the detailed request supplies the background, format and constraints that make the draft usable. The bare request is the tempting runner-up because Claude will produce something fluent, but it will be generic and cost extra rounds of revision.

compare.scenario: A product team needs a launch plan for a leadership review: market sizing, audience segments, messaging, a channel plan and a risk list. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Send one long request that asks for all five sections at once and tell Claude to be thorough about each of them.
compare.optionB: Work in stages: sizing and segments first, then messaging and channels built on the approved segments, then the risk list.
compare.why: The later sections depend on the earlier ones, so a staged chain lets the team inspect and correct segments before messaging is built on them. The single request is the tempting runner-up because it is faster, but errors in the early sections would flow unnoticed into everything after them.

compare.scenario: Claude drafted a competitor summary with eight statistics and named sources, and it goes to the chief executive tomorrow. Which verification approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each statistic and keep the ones it calls high-confidence, then move on.
compare.optionB: Ask Claude for the passage and link behind each statistic, then open each source to confirm the number, year and wording.
compare.why: Checking each figure against its source is independent verification, and asking for the passage makes the check quick. Self-rated confidence is the tempting runner-up because it is fast, but it comes from the same source as the claim and says nothing about whether the source exists or supports the number.

compare.scenario: A ten-page technical report must also reach the executive team, who will decide on a budget request. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Ask for an executive version led by impact and the decision needed, about 150 words, then compare it with the original.
compare.optionB: Ask Claude to 'make it shorter and simpler', check that it reads well, and send the result to the executives.
compare.why: Adapting for an audience works when the reader, need and length are stated, and the comparison with the original catches meaning drift. A plain 'make it shorter' is the tempting runner-up, but it cuts without regard to what executives need and can drop a condition or turn 'may' into 'will' without anyone noticing.

compare.scenario: A manager has limited time to review two Claude drafts: the weekly internal team update and a customer-facing warranty statement. Where should the review effort go?
compare.optionA: Read the internal update line by line and approve the short warranty statement quickly.
compare.optionB: Have legal review the warranty statement carefully and give the internal update a quick read.
compare.why: Verification should be proportional to the consequences of an error, and a warranty statement creates legal and customer exposure that a team update does not. Reading the update closely is the tempting runner-up because it is the longer document, but length is not risk.

compare.scenario: A team lead needs 2,000 short product descriptions rewritten into one consistent format tonight, and speed and cost matter. Which approach is the better one?
compare.optionA: Use a smaller, faster model at modest effort, check a sample, and move up a tier only if quality falls short.
compare.optionB: Use the most capable model tier at maximum effort for every description so that quality is never in doubt.
compare.why: This is straightforward, high-volume work, where the efficient model usually meets the bar and sampling confirms it. The top tier at maximum effort is the tempting runner-up because it feels safe, but it would spend time and allowance on quality the task does not need.

compare.scenario: A director wants a landscape review of five vendors using public sources and internal files in a connected drive, with citations she can open. Which feature is the better fit?
compare.optionA: Web search, asked separately for each vendor and then pieced together by hand.
compare.optionB: Research mode, with web search turned on and the drive connected to the chat.
compare.why: Research mode runs many searches that build on each other across the web and the enabled integrations and returns a cited report, which suits a multi-source review. Web search is the tempting runner-up because it also cites sources and is quicker, but it handles one or two searches at a time and does not combine internal files into a single synthesis.

compare.scenario: An operations team's timing data show that purchase requests wait about three days for a budget check by the approving manager, while keying a request into the system takes ten minutes. The team lead wants Claude to speed things up. Which plan is better?
compare.optionA: Have Claude draft the text entered with each request, because data entry is the most repetitive, text-heavy step.
compare.optionB: Have Claude assemble the budget lines, prior spend and policy flags into a one-page brief for the approving manager, who still decides.
compare.why: Output is limited by the step where work queues up, so improving a step that is not the constraint changes little: shaving minutes off a ten-minute task will not shorten a three-day wait. Preparing the brief targets the measured bottleneck while the manager keeps the decision. Data entry is the tempting runner-up because it looks like the easiest, most text-heavy win.

compare.scenario: A team has built a Claude-assisted workflow for weekly status summaries and now wants colleagues to use it. Which launch plan is better?
compare.optionA: Email the written procedure and a recorded demo to everyone, ask them to start next Monday, and review usage figures after a quarter.
compare.optionB: Run a short hands-on session where staff try the workflow on their own reports, name a go-to person for questions and collect feedback after two weeks.
compare.why: Adoption depends on trust, skills and support, which a hands-on session, a named contact and an early feedback check provide, and problems surface while they are cheap to fix. The email-and-demo launch is the tempting runner-up because it is cheap and documented, but passive material leaves people stuck at the first awkward step, and a quarterly review finds out far too late.

compare.scenario: Finance updates a forecast spreadsheet in the company's shared drive every morning, and an analyst wants Claude's answers to reflect the latest figures. Her Owner has enabled the Google Drive connector and she can open the file. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Upload a fresh copy of the spreadsheet to the chat each morning before asking questions.
compare.optionB: Use the Google Drive connector so that Claude reads the live file within her own permissions.
compare.why: A connector reaches the live file on demand within her permissions, so answers follow the daily updates without a manual step to forget. Uploading is the tempting runner-up because it gives her control over exactly what Claude sees, but every upload is a static copy that is out of date the moment finance edits the original, and a missed upload quietly produces stale answers.

compare.scenario: A finance analyst wants Claude to find spending trends in an export of 6,000 customer transactions that includes customer names and card-account numbers. Company policy restricts personal data in AI tools. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Upload the full export in the approved workspace, with a note telling Claude to ignore the names and account numbers.
compare.optionB: Upload an export that keeps only date, amount, category and region, after checking the file for hidden identifiers.
compare.why: Sending only what the task needs removes the personal data before it is shared, which is what the policy asks for, and the file check covers identifiers hiding in properties or other sheets. The full upload is the tempting runner-up because the workspace is approved and the note sounds careful, but telling Claude to ignore data does not stop the data being shared.

compare.scenario: A recruiter has 400 applications for an analyst role and wants to save time with Claude. Which use is better?
compare.optionA: Have Claude summarize each application against the posted requirements, while the recruiter decides who advances and applicants are told AI supports screening.
compare.optionB: Have Claude rank all the applicants and send automatic rejection emails to the bottom half, so that recruiters see only the best.
compare.why: Hiring is a high-risk area, so a qualified person must be able to review and change every outcome and the affected people should be told that AI is used; summaries keep most of the time saving without Claude making the decision. Automatic ranking and rejection is the tempting runner-up because it saves the most time, but it removes meaningful human review and risks hidden bias such as disparate impact.

compare.scenario: A procurement team's Claude prompt for comparing supplier quotes worked well on six tidy sample quotes, and the team plans to roll it out to all buyers next week. Which plan is better?
compare.optionA: Roll it out to all buyers now, because six successful samples show that the prompt is ready for real use.
compare.optionB: First run it on messy real quotes, such as missing prices, odd currencies and scanned pages, fix what breaks, and then roll it out in stages.
compare.why: Tidy samples hide failures. Unusual inputs show where the prompt breaks before buyers depend on it, and a staged rollout limits the damage from whatever remains. Rolling out at once is the tempting runner-up because the early results look good, but six clean examples say little about real quotes.

compare.scenario: A team keeps reaching its usage limit while preparing weekly client briefings. Which change is better?
compare.optionA: Keep recurring reference documents in a Project, group related questions into single messages, and save high effort for the hardest briefings.
compare.optionB: Move every briefing task to the smallest, cheapest model, whatever the difficulty of the briefing, to stay under the limit.
compare.why: The first change removes waste, such as repeated pasting, one-question-at-a-time messages and effort the task does not need, without lowering quality where it matters. Downgrading every task is the tempting runner-up because it saves allowance quickly, but complex briefings may suffer, and the team would pay for it in rework.
